Topic: rag-and-retrieval

How a system finds the right passages and answers from them, taught from zero: words and vectors, BM25 and embeddings, vector indexes, hybrid search and rerankers, measuring where an answer gets lost, and agentic retrieval. Measured on an Apple M1 Pro with open models and public datasets, with published results kept apart. Data as of October 2026.
0 One screen1 Why retrieve2 Words3 Vectors4 Indexes5 Pipeline6 Where it gets lost7 Who drives8 Production9 Tools10 Child pagesMistakesInterview

Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) means: before a language model answers, a search system finds the few passages of a document collection that bear on the question and pastes them into the model's prompt, so the model answers from text it can read and cite rather than from memory. This page teaches it from zero by following one question from words to vectors to the prompt, finding where its answer gets lost, and then letting the model drive the search itself.

The running example. Every tab of this page measures on the same public data, models and machine, so numbers can be compared across tabs. The main set is SciFact: 5,183 scientific abstracts and 300 test claims (short statements such as "Activation of PPM1D suppresses p53 function"), each with the abstracts human annotators marked as evidence. Three more sets cover what SciFact cannot: NFCorpus (3,633 medical documents, many relevant per query), QASPER (281 long NLP papers, for cutting documents into pieces) and HotpotQA (200 questions that need two Wikipedia paragraphs each, for multi-step search). Everything runs locally on an Apple M1 Pro laptop with open models (four embedding models, three rerankers, Qwen3 1.7B and 4B as the answering model), with no paid APIs. Numbers are labelled: measured means produced here in October 2026 (by this page's tabs or its child pages), vendor a figure a company publishes about its own product, published a paper or independent benchmark, derived computed from other numbers with the formula shown, and illustrative an input chosen for teaching. The definition of the running example, with every model revision and its baseline scores against BEIR and MTEB, is in the page's src/data/README.md.

Where 188 answers go: one pipeline, every claim, stage by stage

not yet decidedlost at retrievallost at rankinglost at generationcorrect, citing evidencedotted square: a CONTRADICT claim

The 188 SciFact test claims that have annotated evidence (124 SUPPORT, 64 CONTRADICT). First stage: BM25 and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, fused with reciprocal rank fusion; reranker: Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B on the top 30; the top 3 abstracts go to Qwen3-1.7B, which must give the right label (SUPPORT, CONTRADICT) and cite an evidence abstract. A deterministic check, no judge. measured on Apple M1 Pro, recorded by the Pipeline lab (src/pipe/out/e2e.json).

Read the picture as the whole page in miniature. A first stage looks at all 5,183 abstracts and keeps a shortlist; a reranker reads the shortlist carefully and reorders it; only the top few reach the generator (the language model that writes the answer). An abstract that falls out at any stage is gone for good. Here the first two stages almost never fail (186 of 188 claims have their evidence in the top 30, and 178 keep it in the top 3); the answering model fails on 82 of the 178 claims whose evidence it was given. Every one of the 59 CONTRADICT claims that reached the prompt was answered wrongly: the 1.7 B model never said CONTRADICT with abstracts in front of it. One accuracy number (96 of 188) would hide all of that.

Five ideas carry everything that follows.

1. Words and vectors
miss different things

Keyword search (BM25) finds exact names; embeddings find paraphrases. SciFact nDCG@10 (a 0 to 1 score of how high the right abstracts sit in the top 10, defined in section 6): BM25 0.679, Qwen3-Embedding 0.700, the two fused 0.724. Sections 2, 3, 5.

2. Recall first
lost early, lost for good

Nothing downstream can use a passage the first stage never returned, so the first stage is tuned to keep the right passage somewhere in a long list. Sections 4, 5.

3. Read the shortlist twice
0.724 to 0.778

A reranker that reads query and passage together lifts the fused list on SciFact, but only if it is stronger than the first stage. Section 5.

4. Measure the factors
A = r × p × g

Accuracy is found, kept, then used. Measured apart, each points at its own fix. Section 6.

5. Who drives
pipeline or loop

A fixed pipeline searches once; an agent searches as often as it judges it needs. On 200 two-hop questions with Qwen3-4B the loop gains 0.084 F1 for about 3 times the tokens and seconds. Section 7.

A = rK × pk|K × g
A
end-to-end accuracy: share of questions answered correctly for the right reason (citing evidence)
rK
share whose evidence is in the first stage's top K (here K = 30): 186 / 188 = 0.989
pk|K
of those, share whose evidence the reranker keeps in the top k that reach the prompt (k = 3): 178 / 186 = 0.957
g
of those, share the generator answers correctly: 96 / 178 = 0.539; so A = 0.989 × 0.957 × 0.539 = 0.511 = 96 / 188

Two reference points measured: given only the gold abstracts (an "oracle" prompt), the same model and prompt get 112 of 188, the ceiling of g; with no abstracts at all ("closed book") it gets the label right on 45 of 188 and can cite nothing. Section 6 turns this into a method.

1. Why retrieve at all

What a model knows against what it can read. A language model's weights hold a compressed, lossy memory of its training text (its parametric memory): frozen at a cutoff date, with no record of where any fact came from, and silent about what it never saw. Its context window is different: whatever text is placed in the prompt is read now, exactly, and can be quoted. Retrieval moves knowledge from the first place to the second. That buys four things, each measured on this page:

  • Grounding. Closed book, Qwen3-1.7B gets the SciFact label right on 45 of 188 claims and has nothing to cite; with the gold abstracts in the prompt it gets 112 right and cites them measured.
  • Freshness. Updating knowledge means re-indexing documents, not retraining weights. It is not free: the index must be refreshed (Elasticsearch makes new documents searchable after its default refresh interval of 1 s, per its index-module docs as read by the production child), deleted text can survive in index files (the RAG in production child found a deleted row's text still in pgvector's table and HNSW files until VACUUM FULL measured), and a new embedding model means re-embedding everything (section 8).
  • Citations. The system knows which passages it put in the prompt, so it can show them, and a checker can verify that the answer cites one of them, as the SciFact check above does.
  • Access control. Only retrieval can give each user a different view of the same corpus. It has to happen at retrieval, not in the prompt (predict below).
Predict: a restricted document is retrieved into the prompt, and the system prompt says "never reveal restricted documents to this user". The user asks about it. Of 18 such questions, how many answers leak the restricted fact (Qwen3-1.7B and 4B, a constructed company corpus)?
17 of 18 for both models. With the document filtered out at retrieval instead, 0 of 18. The RAG in production child also planted an instruction inside a public document: the 1.7 B model followed it in 6 of 6 cases with a plain prompt measured on Apple M1 Pro. Text in the context window is read as text; a rule in the prompt is not a security boundary.

The corpus can matter more than the model. The old version of this page quoted OpenAI's Astra for Law (September 2026): GPT-6 Astra plus a legal index of more than 230 million URLs built on CourtListener, 54% against 38.7% for the same model with ordinary web search on the Vals AI Legal Research Bench vendor. The lesson stands, with two corrections from the Topic: benchmarks page's check (read 2026-10-04): the product also adds legal instructions and was scored on OpenAI's private validation set, so the index's own effect is not isolated; and Vals AI's public leaderboard lists GPT-6 Astra at 39.42% with no Astra for Law entry. So: a retrieval-sensitive score quoted without its index carries little information, and a vendor's own split of the gain is a claim, not a measurement.

2. Words: tokens, the inverted index, BM25

The problem. Given a query and millions of documents, return the few that contain its answer, in milliseconds, without reading every document.

Tokens. First, text becomes a list of terms: split into words, lowercase, drop very common stopwords ("the", "of", and in Lucene's English list also "no" and "not"), and cut each word to a stem so that "decreases" and "decreased" match ("decreas"). The claim "Statins decrease blood cholesterol." becomes statin decreas blood cholesterol. These are search terms, not the subword tokens a language model uses (Tokenizers).

The inverted index. Like the index at the back of a book: for each term, the list of documents containing it and how often (its postings list). A query reads only its terms' lists. Document frequency (df) is the length of a term's list: in SciFact, "statin" appears in 23 of 5,183 abstracts, "decreas" in 573.

Scoring: TF-IDF, then BM25. Two intuitions. A rare term is strong evidence (matching "statin" says more than matching "decreas"): weight each term by its inverse document frequency, IDF, large when df is small. A term repeated in a document is evidence it is about that term, but with diminishing returns, and a long document repeats everything more. TF-IDF multiplies term frequency by IDF; BM25 (Best Match 25, Robertson and colleagues, 1990s) adds the saturation and the length correction, and is still the standard keyword scorer:

score(D, Q) = Σt ∈ Q IDF(t) · tf · (k1 + 1) / (tf + k1(1 − b + b · |D| / avgdl))
tf
how often term t occurs in document D
IDF(t)
ln(1 + (N − df + 0.5) / (df + 0.5)), with N documents in the corpus (Lucene's form)
k1
saturation: how fast repeats stop adding (1.2 here)
b
length normalisation: 0 ignores length, 1 fully divides by it (0.75 here)
|D|, avgdl
the document's length in terms, and the corpus average (156.7 terms in SciFact)

bm25s, used here, and Lucene since version 8 drop the constant factor (k1 + 1); it multiplies every score by the same number and does not change the order. The scores below are bm25s's, so they match the recorded run. How engines store and compress postings, and BM25 inside PostgreSQL, are on Search and vector databases.

BM25 on a real claim: why the relevant abstract comes third

Claim 1099 of the SciFact test set; the two abstracts are BM25's first and third results (the second is not shown). Term counts and lengths from the bm25s index of the running example, as extracted by the retrieval pipeline child; at the defaults the page recomputes the recorded scores 8.963 and 7.366 exactly measured, derived when you move a slider.

What it costs, and when it matters. BM25 needs no model and no GPU: 0.25 ms per SciFact query here, against 49 ms just to embed the query with Qwen3-Embedding measured, M1 Pro. It is strong whenever queries share exact words with the answer: identifiers, gene names, error codes, product numbers. On SciFact it scores nDCG@10 0.679, better than the small MiniLM embedding model (0.645). It fails on paraphrase: an abstract that says "lowers LDL" never matches "decrease cholesterol". How to check it: the tokeniser matters more than the BM25 variant (rank_bm25's Okapi BM25 on the same tokens scores 0.684; the BEIR paper's Elasticsearch BM25, with another analyser, 0.665 published); and tuning k1 and b on SciFact's training claims changes the test score by 0.001 (the retrieval pipeline child's grid). Leave the defaults; fix the tokeniser first.

3. Vectors: embeddings, similarity, training

The problem. The claim "Mitochondria are uninvolved in apoptosis" should find an abstract about cytochrome c release triggering programmed cell death, which shares almost none of its words. Matching meaning needs a representation of meaning that can be compared fast.

How it works. An embedding model is a neural network that reads a text and outputs a fixed-length list of numbers, a vector (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B outputs 1,024; bge-small 384). It is trained so that a query and the passages that answer it land close together. Each number means nothing alone; only distances carry information. Dense retrieval embeds every document once, embeds the query at search time, and returns the nearest documents. Because query and document are encoded separately, document vectors are computed ahead of time: this kind of model is a bi-encoder. (A cross-encoder, section 5, reads the two together: more accurate, nothing to precompute.)

Similarity. Three ways to compare vectors q and d: the dot product Σ qidi (larger is closer, and it grows with the vectors' lengths), cosine (the dot product divided by both lengths: only the angle counts) and L2 distance |q − d| (smaller is closer). If every vector has length 1, then cosine = dot and |q − d|2 = 2 − 2 cos, so all three give the same order. Most models normalise their output; gte-modernbert-base does not. On its raw vectors, SciFact nDCG@10 is 0.767 by cosine, 0.767 by L2 and 0.740 by dot product: the dot product silently loses 0.027 because it favours long vectors measured, Vector search lab. Normalise once at write time, then any of the three is the same search.

Scores are not probabilities, and not comparable across models. On one batch of eight SciFact training claims and their abstracts, bge-small's cosines run from 0.43 to 0.79 and Qwen3-Embedding's from 0.14 to 0.70; the median cosine of random pairs is 0.563 for bge-small and 0.097 for MiniLM measured. "Keep results above 0.7" means something different for each model, and changes silently when you swap models. Thresholds are tuned per model on labelled data.

How embedding models are trained

Pairs of (query, passage that answers it) are collected: questions and answers, titles and bodies, search queries and clicked pages, and, in modern recipes, pairs written by a language model (Qwen3-Embedding's report describes about 150 million synthetic pairs in a first stage vendor). The loss is InfoNCE: for each query, a softmax over its similarity to its own passage and to a line-up of wrong ones, and the loss is minus the log-probability of the right one. It is a classification where the classes are the candidates.

Li = − log [ exp(cos(qi, di+) / τ) / Σj exp(cos(qi, dj) / τ) ]
di+
the passage that answers query i
dj
every candidate: the positive, the other queries' positives in the batch (in-batch negatives, free because they are already embedded) and any hard negatives (mined passages that look relevant but are not)
τ
temperature: small values make small cosine gaps matter (SimCSE used 0.05)

Bigger batches mean a harder line-up: bge-small's positive outscores all in-batch negatives for 97.9% of SciFact training claims at batch size 8 and for 82.8% at 512 measured. Hard negatives teach fine distinctions but carry a trap, the false negative: for 38.8% of SciFact's training claims (bge-small) the corpus holds an unlabelled abstract that outscores the labelled one, and some of those are relevant abstracts nobody labelled. Training on them pushes right answers away. The general theory of contrastive losses is on Contrastive and self-supervised learning; the loss computed live on a real batch is in the Vector search lab; fine-tuning a model on your own data belongs to the Embedding models child.

Query instructions. Many models expect a prefix on queries only (bge-small: "Represent this sentence for searching relevant passages: "; Qwen3-Embedding: "Instruct: task\nQuery:"). Measure it: bge-small's prefix is within noise here (SciFact 0.720 without, 0.713 with; NFCorpus 0.337 without, 0.343 with), while dropping Qwen3-Embedding's instruction costs 2.1 points on SciFact and 6.6 on NFCorpus measured, Embedding models child.

Which model: what MTEB measures, and what it does not

MTEB (Massive Text Embedding Benchmark) scores embedding models on dozens of tasks; its retrieval tasks use nDCG@10, mostly on BEIR datasets used zero-shot (the model never trained on them). The headline is an average over task types, many models trained on the benchmarks' training splits (Qwen3-Embedding declares HotpotQA and FEVER, so its HotpotQA results here are in-domain, not zero-shot), and gaps under a point are noise. The Tool map explains each of these. The chart shows why your own data decides:

Five retrievers, three datasets: the order changes

nDCG@10 on each test set, exact search, deterministic measured; every embedding model is within 0.005 of its published MTEB number on SciFact and NFCorpus (src/data/README.md). Multi-hop: 200 HotpotQA questions over the running example's 9,760 paragraphs, relevance = the two gold paragraphs; Qwen3-Embedding trained on HotpotQA (in-domain).

What transfers. Model size is not a ranking: the 149 M gte-modernbert beats the 0.6 B Qwen3-Embedding on SciFact (0.767 against 0.700), Qwen3 wins NFCorpus, and bge-small (33 M) wins the multi-hop set. Cost scales with size: per document, Qwen3-Embedding indexes about 20 times slower than bge-small here (6.4 against 144 documents per second on MPS) measured, roughly its parameter ratio, on any hardware. Shortlist on the retrieval tasks closest to your domain, then measure nDCG@10 and recall@100 on a few hundred of your own labelled queries.

4. Indexes: finding the nearest vectors fast

Exact search first. Exact (flat, brute-force) search compares the query with every stored vector and keeps the best k. It is always right and needs no index. On one core of this laptop it streams about 37 GB of vectors per second: 0.5 ms for SciFact's 5,183 vectors of 1,024 numbers, 22 ms for 522,931 Quora questions of 384 numbers, about 112 ms for a million of 1,024 measured, Vector indexes child. Below roughly a million vectors, exact search is often fast enough, and it is always the honest baseline that every approximate index is measured against.

The memory bill, and what an exact scan costs

Vector bytes = vectors × dimensions × bytes per number derived. Graph: hnswlib's layer 0 keeps up to 2M neighbour ids of 4 bytes plus a 4-byte count per vector (upper layers hold about 1 in M vectors and are left out) derived from the layout read in hnswlib 0.8.0 by the Vector indexes child. Scan time = vector bytes / 37 GB/s, the one-core rate measured for float32 on this M1 Pro; at the defaults it gives 111 ms against the child's measured 112 ms (by construction, since the rate came from that run). Real engines add metadata, text and allocator overhead.

Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes look at a small part of the data and accept that they will sometimes miss a true neighbour. Three ideas cover almost every index in use, each shown here with one measured number on SciFact's Qwen3-Embedding vectors (share of the exact top 10 returned, called ANN recall@10) measured:

  • IVF (inverted file): k-means splits the vectors into cells; a query scans only the nprobe cells nearest to it. With 72 cells, scanning 1 cell returns 0.482 of the true top 10, 8 cells 0.901, 32 cells 0.992. It misses neighbours just across a cell border.
  • PQ (product quantization): cut each vector into m pieces and replace each piece by the id of its nearest learned centroid, so 4,096 bytes become m bytes, and distances are estimated from the codes. At 16 bytes per vector: 0.450 alone, 0.914 after rescoring the top 100 with the full vectors. IVF-PQ combines both, the classic billion-scale design.
  • HNSW (hierarchical navigable small world, Malkov and Yashunin): link each vector to a few near neighbours, in layers from sparse to dense; a query walks greedily toward closer vectors keeping a frontier of efSearch candidates. FAISS HNSW (M 32): efSearch 16 returns 0.980, efSearch 64 0.999. It is the graph index of pgvector, Qdrant, Weaviate, Milvus and Lucene, and costs memory for the graph.
  • DiskANN (Vamana graph): one flat graph kept on SSD with compressed vectors in memory, for collections larger than RAM (Subramanya et al., NeurIPS 2019 published). Not runnable on this Mac (diskannpy ships Linux and Windows wheels only); the Vector indexes child built Vamana from the paper's algorithms instead.

Smaller vectors. Two knobs, independent: fewer bits per number, or fewer numbers. Storing Qwen3-Embedding's vectors as int8 (1 byte each) and searching with a float query returns 0.996 of the exact top 10; binary codes (1 bit each, 32 times smaller) return only 0.674, and 0.990 after rescoring the top 100 with the float vectors. Matryoshka training (Kusupati et al. 2022) packs the most useful information into the first dimensions so vectors can be cut: Qwen3-Embedding, trained that way, keeps 98% of its nDCG at half its dimensions and 95% at a quarter; bge-small, not trained that way, keeps 94% and 81% measured, Vector search lab. Binary needs rescoring; int8 with a float query is close to free; truncation works for models trained for it.

Predict: an HNSW setting returns 95.9% of the exact top 10 (efSearch 8). Exact search finds a labelled relevant abstract in the top 10 for 84.5% of claims. With this index, about how often?
82.7%. These are two different recalls. ANN recall asks how much of the exact top 10 the index returned: it needs no labels and measures only the index. Retrieval recall asks how many labelled relevant documents are in the top 10: it measures the embedding model first and the index second. The index loses relevant abstracts at about the rate it loses any neighbour (IVF with 8 cells: ANN 0.901, retrieval 0.779 against 0.761 expected from 0.901 × 0.845) measured. A perfect index cannot lift retrieval above the model's 0.845.

Filters. Real queries carry conditions (tenant, date, permissions). Applying the filter after the index (a post-filter) is easy and silently returns fewer results: when a user may see 10% of SciFact, fetching 10 and filtering leaves 1.73 on average and nothing at all for 14 of 300 claims measured, Pipeline lab. Filtering inside the search is the fix, and with a graph index it has its own failure: a restrictive filter cuts the paths the walk needs. Engines add iterative scans (pgvector since 0.8.0), filter-aware traversal (ACORN, Weaviate's default since v1.34) or a switch to exact search when few rows pass. The Vector indexes child measures all of these, and Search and vector databases shows them inside PostgreSQL.

Stores, and the index you did not get. A vector store wraps an index with storage, metadata and filtering. Small test collections can hide the index entirely: the Qdrant 1.19.2 server builds no HNSW graph for a collection under its 10,000 KB indexing threshold, and even with the graph built its planner scans exactly below a second 10,000 KB threshold, so SciFact (about 8 MB of bge-small vectors) was always searched exactly; Milvus Lite scans flat even after you ask for HNSW measured, Tool map. Benchmark the server and the size you will run. The atlas of stores, with what index each actually runs, is the Tool map; the Vector search lab shows exact against HNSW against IVF-PQ on one query.

5. The pipeline: chunk, rewrite, fuse, filter, rerank, assemble

A production retrieval pipeline runs in two halves. At index time, before any question: parse documents, cut them into chunks, attach metadata, write a keyword index and a vector index. At query time: rewrite the question if it needs it, search both indexes with the filters inside each search, fuse the two lists, rerank the top of the fused list, and put the best few chunks, with their ids, into the prompt. Each stage below has the problem it solves, what it costs, and one measured lesson. The Pipeline lab measures every stage on the running example; the retrieval pipeline and rerankers children go deeper.

Chunking: cut where the author did, compare at equal tokens

A paper is thousands of tokens; an embedding model reads a few hundred, and the prompt holds a few passages. So documents are cut into chunks, each indexed on its own. If a cut falls through the paragraph that answers the question, no chunk holds the whole answer. On QASPER's 892 questions with annotated evidence paragraphs, fixed 256-token windows keep an evidence paragraph whole for 607 (68.0%); splitting on blank lines first (the "recursive" rule) keeps 838 (93.9%) measured. Overlap between windows is a patch: 32 tokens of it move fixed windows from 546 to 607 and cost 14% more tokens to index.

The trap is in how chunkers are compared. At a fixed number of chunks (the top 3), 512-token fixed chunks beat paragraph-aware chunks of at most 256 tokens with BM25 (61.4% of questions found against 45.3%), because three 512-token chunks are three times the text. At an equal budget of 1,024 tokens the order flips: 45.9% against 64.5% measured. Compare chunkers at an equal token budget. Before chunking comes parsing PDFs into text: of 107 evidence paragraphs in QASPER papers' PDFs, MinerU (flash) kept 94 intact and pdfplumber 1 (Document ingestion child) measured.

Contextual retrieval (Anthropic, September 2024) has a language model write one or two sentences situating each chunk in its document, prepended before indexing; Anthropic reports top-20 retrieval failures falling from 5.7% to 3.7% with contextual embeddings, 2.9% adding contextual BM25 and 1.9% adding a reranker, at $1.02 per million document tokens with prompt caching vendor. Run here with Qwen3-1.7B writing the context on 71 QASPER papers, it gave no clear gain (bge-small at a 1,024-token budget 57.7% to 55.2%, within noise) measured: the writer's quality matters, and the setting differs (here retrieval runs inside one paper).

Query transformation

The words a user types are not always the documents' words. HyDE (Gao et al. 2022) asks the model to write a fake answer passage and embeds that; multi-query retrieves with several rewordings and fuses; conversational rewrite turns "does it help?" into a standalone question using the chat history. On SciFact, HyDE lifts Qwen3-Embedding from 0.700 to 0.718, multi-query does nothing (0.699), and each costs a generator call before retrieval can start (about 2.2 s and 0.8 s per claim with the 1.7 B model here, more than the whole retrieval stage) measured. On eight constructed two-turn chats, the rewrite put the evidence in the top 3 for 6 to 7 of 8, against 3 to 5 for the follow-up alone. Rewrite in chat always; gate the rest on query difficulty.

Hybrid search and reciprocal rank fusion

BM25 and embeddings make different mistakes, so production systems run both and merge the lists. The scores live on different scales (a BM25 score of 9 against a cosine of 0.7), so the standard merge ignores scores and uses ranks: reciprocal rank fusion (RRF; Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009) gives each document Σlists 1 / (k + rank), with k = 60. A document both lists rank moderately beats one list's favourite.

Hybrid helps some models and hurts others; a reranker helps only if it is stronger

SciFact, 300 test claims, nDCG@10, deterministic measured, Pipeline lab (src/pipe/out/fusion.json and rerank.json). Fused list: BM25 + Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B with RRF k 60. Rerankers read the fused top K and the rest of the list keeps its order.

Equal-weight RRF helps a dense model that is about as good as BM25 and disagrees with it (MiniLM 0.645 to 0.713, Qwen3-Embedding 0.700 to 0.724) and hurts the two that clearly beat BM25 (gte-modernbert 0.767 to 0.763, ColBERT-small 0.743 to 0.731): equal weight gives the weaker list the same say. A weighted fusion with the weight chosen on SciFact's training claims (z-score fusion, α 0.6) reaches 0.739 for Qwen3; picking α on the test claims would claim 0.744, a leak. Hybrid is not always better; measure it, and tune any weight on held-out queries.

Filtering

Metadata filters go inside each first-stage search, never on a list already cut to a top-k (section 4 has the measured loss). Access control is a filter, and the only place it works is here (section 1).

Reranking, and late interaction

A cross-encoder reranker puts the query and one candidate through a single transformer together and outputs one relevance score. It sees every interaction between their words, so it is far more accurate than comparing two precomputed vectors, and far too slow for the whole corpus, so it reads only the first stage's top K. Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B lifts the fused list from 0.724 to 0.782 at K 20; bge-reranker-v2-m3 reaches 0.757; the small ms-marco MiniLM cross-encoder, trained on web search, makes it worse the deeper it reads (0.702 at K 30, 0.689 at K 100). It reproduces the BEIR paper's BM25+CE score (0.688) only because BM25 alone is weaker than it. A reranker helps only when it is stronger than the first stage. The price is time and grows linearly with K: at K 30, 155 ms for MiniLM, 2.18 s for bge-reranker-v2-m3 and 6.62 s for Qwen3-Reranker on this laptop's GPU, batch 1 measured.

Late interaction (ColBERT) sits between the two: keep one small vector per token of every document, and score a query by summing, for each query token, its best match among the document's tokens (MaxSim). answerai-colbert-small scores 0.743 on SciFact searching exhaustively, at 29 times the storage of one bge-small vector per abstract measured, rerankers child. The rerankers child covers cross-encoders in code, depth, calibration, LLM rerankers, ColBERT and PLAID.

Prompt assembly and citations

The top k chunks go into the prompt with stable ids, and the instruction asks the model to answer from them and cite the id it used, which makes the answer checkable. Two measured lessons. The prompt is a knob, tuned on held-out data like any other: the Pipeline lab's first SciFact prompt made Qwen3-1.7B answer "NOT ENOUGH INFO" almost always (23 of 188 right even with the gold abstracts); three prompts were compared on training claims, and the chosen one gets 112 with gold abstracts. More context is not free for a small model: with the reranker on, g falls from 0.626 with one abstract to 0.539 with three and 0.530 with five measured. Where in a long prompt the evidence sits matters too (section 7).

6. Where an answer gets lost, and how to measure it

The golden set. Every number above needs a golden set: real questions, each with the passages a human marked as answering it (and, for judging answers, a reference answer). A few hundred real, labelled questions separate systems that differ by a few points; synthetic questions written from a chunk are easy by construction, because they reuse the chunk's words. Version the set, re-label when the corpus is re-chunked, choose every knob (fusion weight, rerank depth, prompt) on a separate tuning split, and report the test split once. SciFact here: 809 training claims for tuning, 300 test claims for reporting.

Retrieval metrics, per question then averaged (computed here with pytrec_eval, the TREC tool BEIR uses):

  • recall@K: the share of a question's relevant passages in the top K. With one relevant passage (277 of 300 SciFact claims) it is simply "found or not".
  • precision@k: the share of the top k that is relevant; irrelevant chunks in the prompt distract the generator.
  • MRR (mean reciprocal rank): 1 / rank of the first relevant passage, averaged.
  • nDCG@10 (normalised discounted cumulative gain): each relevant passage in the top 10 earns its relevance grade divided by log2(rank + 1), and the sum is divided by the best possible sum, so 1 is a perfect order. It rewards putting the right passage first, which is what a reranker is for.

Measure the first stage's recall at the depth the reranker reads (K), not only at the k that reaches the prompt: a reranker cannot rescue what it was never given, and the two depths separate a retrieval miss from a ranking miss. The formulas, a calculator on real BEIR runs and the LLM-judged metrics (faithfulness, answer relevance, context precision and recall) belong to RAG and retrieval evaluation; judge design and bias to LLM-as-judge.

The decomposition. A question is answered correctly for the right reason only if its evidence survives three stages in a row, so end-to-end accuracy over N questions factors as A = rK × pk|K × g (section 0), and the N(1 − A) failures split into three buckets that add up exactly:

Mretrieval = N(1 − r)   Mranking = N r (1 − p)   Mgeneration = N r p (1 − g)
Mretrieval
evidence never reached the reranker: fix chunking, hybrid search, query rewriting, or raise K
Mranking
reached the reranker, not the prompt: a better reranker, or a larger k
Mgeneration
in the prompt, answered wrongly: the model, the prompt, the context format, abstention instructions

It assumes the answer needs its evidence; an answer right from the model's own memory is not counted as right, which is why the SciFact check also requires a cited evidence abstract (4 claims got the right label with no evidence in the prompt and were refused measured). Without the citation check a label is cheap: two thirds of the labelled claims are SUPPORT, so always answering SUPPORT would score 66%.

Price the levers: which factor is worth fixing?

Arithmetic only derived. Presets: the measured run of section 0 (N 188, r 186/188, p 178/186, g 96/178) and the old version of this page's illustrative golden set (N 200, r 0.9, p 0.833, g 0.9), whose figures the calculator reproduces: A 0.675, buckets 20, 30 and 15, and perfect-factor accuracies 0.75, 0.75 and 0.81.

On the measured run the generation bucket is 82 of 92 failures: no retrieval change can buy more than 10 answers, while the oracle run (gold abstracts only, 112 of 188) shows how much a better prompt or model could. On the old example the ranking bucket was the largest. The point of measuring the factors is that the instinct ("try a bigger model") is right in one case and wrong in the other. How to debug one bad answer: log, per question, the first stage's top K, the reranked top k and the answer; ask first "was the evidence in the prompt?", then "was it in the top K?"; that one or two bits assign the failure to a stage before anyone touches a component.

7. Who drives retrieval: pipelines, agents, graphs, long context, memory

Everything so far is a fixed pipeline: the engineer decided in advance to search once, with the user's words, and to pass the top k on. Three rungs of a ladder differ in who decides what to retrieve:

  • Naive RAG: nobody decides. Embed the question, take the top k, generate.
  • Advanced RAG: the designer decides, in advance, for every question: the rewrite, hybrid search, filter and rerank stages of section 5.
  • Agentic retrieval: the model decides, at run time. Search is a tool it may call zero or more times, with queries it writes itself, reading each result before deciding whether to search again or answer. This is the reason-then-act loop of ReAct; the "deep research" products are the same loop with a budget of minutes.

The problem a loop solves: the second hop. Two questions from HotpotQA's dev set. "Who was born first, Arthur Conan Doyle or Penelope Lively?" (a comparison question) needs two paragraphs, and both names are in the question. "What government position was held by the woman who portrayed Corliss Archer in the film Kiss and Tell?" (a bridge question) needs a paragraph about the film, to learn the actress's name, before the paragraph about her can be searched for: the second paragraph shares almost no words with the question. On the running example's 200 HotpotQA questions, searching once with bge-small puts at least one of the two gold paragraphs in the top 10 for 199 questions, but both for 164; for the 160 bridge questions, 124; for the 40 comparison questions, all 40. BM25: 147 of 200 with both measured, Agentic lab. A single search is good at the first hop and weak at the second, which is exactly what a loop can fix by searching for the name it just learned.

What it costs. Each call of the loop re-reads everything before it: the instructions, the question and every result so far. Without prompt caching, the input tokens over n searches and a final answer are

Tin = (n + 1) s + r · n(n + 1) / 2
n
searches before the answer, so n + 1 model calls
s
tokens every call re-reads: system prompt, tool description, question
r
tokens each search result adds; the call after search i re-reads i results

The n(n + 1)/2 term makes the bill grow quadratically with the number of searches. A prompt cache lowers the price of the re-read prefix, not the time to generate each step.

The same question, a pipeline against an agent loop: input tokens per model call

Formula above, illustrative inputs: s = 1,500 and r = 2,000 tokens, against a pipeline that reads s plus R = 4,000 retrieved tokens once. At 3 searches the agent reads 18,000 tokens (3.3 times the pipeline), at 6 searches 52,500 (9.5 times), the old version of this page's worked example, reproduced derived. The Agentic lab replays real recorded trajectories of Qwen3 models with their measured token counts.

Measured here: the five ways to answer, with Qwen3-4B. The Agentic lab ran each strategy on the 200 HotpotQA questions (search tool: bge-small over the 9,760 paragraphs; temperature 0; F1 is HotpotQA's official token-overlap score of the answer):

StrategyF1searchesinput
tokens		seconds
No retrieval (closed book)0.1930560.28
Single search, top 5 into the prompt0.49017491.98
Agent loop (ReAct, search as a tool)0.5742.192,318
1,046 newly computed		6.15
Fixed decomposition into sub-questions0.48821,9395.65
Long context: the question's own 10 paragraphs0.57601,4703.95
Long context: an 8,000-token window0.47507,95828.77

Means per question, Qwen3-4B Q4_K_M in llama.cpp on the M1 Pro, prompt cache on measured, Agentic lab (src/agent/out/strategies.json). "Newly computed": tokens the prompt cache did not already hold. The 1.7 B rows are left out until a rerun: a prompt bug made that model answer yes or no to non-yes/no questions in its one-call runs.

The loop beats the single search by 0.084 F1 (paired over the same questions, 95% interval 0.022 to 0.144; better on 51, worse on 24) for about 3 times the input tokens and seconds. A fixed decomposition, which plans its sub-questions before seeing any result, buys nothing (0.488). Long context over the question's own 10 paragraphs, which always contain both gold paragraphs, matches the loop (0.576); widened to 8,000 tokens of mostly distractors it drops to 0.475 and takes 29 s per question. The quadratic growth is real: a question that ends after two model calls bills 820 input tokens, one that uses all five 5,370, and those long trajectories are the failures (29 questions used all four searches and score F1 0.18, against 0.673 for the 112 that stopped after two). A step cap does not just bound cost: past two or three searches the small model was mostly lost.

What the published comparisons say. The most careful controlled comparison (Ferrazzi et al., "Is Agentic RAG worth it?", revised April 2026) ran an enhanced pipeline (router, rewriter, retriever, reranker) against an agentic system on the same tasks: its Table 9 gives the agent 2.7 and 3.6 times the input tokens (about 3.15 times on average; its text says 3.3), 1.7 and 1.8 times the output tokens (about 1.75; the text says 1.9) and about 1.5 times the time on its two datasets. The agent won on query rewriting (+2.8 nDCG@10 on average) and lost on deciding whether a query needs retrieval at all: user-intent F1 on FEVER 64.6 against the pipeline's semantic router at 87.9 (Table 3; the agent retrieved when it should not have) published. IRCoT (Trivedi et al. 2022), which interleaves retrieval with reasoning steps, raised HotpotQA answer F1 from 53.6 with one retrieval to 60.7 with GPT-3 published. The loop pays on multi-hop and exploratory questions, and wastes tokens on lookups a single search answers.

Routers. Hence a cheap classifier or rule in front: easy questions to the pipeline, hard ones to the loop. Adaptive-RAG (Jeong et al. 2024) trained a small T5 classifier to pick no retrieval, one search or many: with FLAN-T5-XL it kept most of multi-step retrieval's accuracy (46.94 against 48.85 F1) at about 2.4 times less time, although the classifier itself was right only 54.5% of the time; an oracle router would have reached 56.28 published. A router is worth measuring on your own mix of questions. The Agentic lab built two on a mixed set of 99 single-hop and 100 multi-hop questions (a logistic classifier on question embeddings, and a prompt to the model itself) and compared them with always-pipeline, always-agent and an oracle; the pipeline half of that comparison used the 1.7 B model with the faulty prompt, so its numbers are left out here until the rerun.

GraphRAG: questions about the whole corpus

Some questions have no passage that answers them: "what are the main themes across these 10,000 reports?". Retrieving the top 10 chunks samples ten fragments of the answer. GraphRAG (Edge et al., Microsoft, arXiv 2404.16130) pays at index time instead: a language model reads every chunk and extracts entities and relations into a graph, the Leiden algorithm splits the graph into a hierarchy of communities, the model summarises each community, and a global question is answered map-reduce style over the summaries. On two corpora of about 1 and 1.7 million tokens its global approaches were judged more comprehensive than vector RAG's in 72 to 83% of pairwise comparisons (by an LLM judge) and indexing the first corpus took 281 minutes with gpt-4-turbo published. Cheaper variants: LightRAG (a flat graph with dual graph and vector retrieval; in its own paper it beats GraphRAG overall on three of four datasets by small margins and loses on the fourth, 49.6 against 50.4) published; LazyGraphRAG, which Microsoft says costs the same to index as vector RAG and over 700 times less per global query than GraphRAG's global search vendor, and ships only in Microsoft's products (the Tool map checked the open graphrag 3.3.0 package). Cost figures quoted around the web for a "500-page corpus" ($50 to $200 for GraphRAG, $0.50 for LightRAG) carry no method or source and are not repeated here as facts. For lookups, hybrid search with a reranker is cheaper and at least as good. Measured at small scale: the Agentic lab had Qwen3-1.7B extract entities and relations from 394 HotpotQA paragraphs (53,062 tokens of text): 161,797 generator tokens (about 3 tokens of work per token indexed) and 951 s of generation, about 6.5 hours for the whole 9,760-paragraph corpus at that rate. Retrieving through the graph (dense hits, then one hop along shared entities) put both gold paragraphs in the top 3 for 29 of the first 40 test questions against 26 for dense search alone, and changed nothing at k = 2 or 5; one global "main themes" question by community map-reduce cost 93 model calls and about 20,000 tokens, against one call for a top-10 answer measured, Agentic lab. The GraphRAG and structured retrieval child goes further.

Long context instead of retrieval

If the corpus fits in the context window, why search? Because every query pays for every token. Cost per query C = pin Tfresh + pcache Tcached + pout Tout. With illustrative prices of $3 per million input tokens, $0.30 cached and $15 output, a 1-million-token corpus, a 500-token question and a 500-token answer: RAG with 10 chunks of 400 tokens costs $0.021; putting the whole corpus in the window $3.009 uncached (143 times) and $0.309 with the corpus cached (15 times) derived. Prefill (reading the input before the first output token) takes seconds: Qwen3-1.7B here needs 9.3 s for 7,611 prompt tokens measured, production child. Accuracy is not guaranteed either: in "Lost in the middle" (Liu et al. 2023, Table 6) GPT-3.5-Turbo answered 75.8% of questions with the answer document first among 20, 53.8% with it tenth, below its 56.1% with no documents at all; NoLiMa (2025) found 11 models below half their short-context score at 32K tokens once the question and the answer stop sharing words, GPT-4o falling from 99.3% to 69.7% published. Li et al. (arXiv 2501.01880) found long context generally ahead on question answering (most on Wikipedia questions) and retrieval ahead on dialogue and general questions. Long context wins for a small corpus read once or holistically; retrieval wins on cost, latency, scale beyond the window and per-user access control, and the two compose: retrieve, then read generously. Reproduced at small scale: with the two gold paragraphs placed among 20, Qwen3-4B scores F1 0.682 with them first, 0.540 at positions 5 and 6, 0.554 at 10 and 11, then 0.599 and 0.592 toward the end (100 questions; intervals about ±0.09, so the dip is clear only against the first position) measured, Agentic lab; Long-context and multimodal benchmarks covers how long-context claims are tested.

Retrieval for an agent's own memory

Agent memory is retrieval turned inward: the corpus is the agent's own history, written by the same process that will later need it. Retrieval over memories is the easy part; deciding what to write, how to update or expire a fact, and when to surface it are the hard parts. Two papers in this knowledge base, both corrected against the papers themselves: the Proactive Memory Agent (Meta AI, arXiv 2607.08716) runs a second model that decides when to remind the acting agent, lifting Terminal-Bench 2.0 from 37.6% to 45.9% with Claude Sonnet 4.5 acting and Opus 4.6 reminding published; Just-in-Time Memory keeps raw trajectories and curates them when a task arrives, +16.2 points on ALFWorld over RL-trained SkillOS, but most of that comes from training the curator, not from the timing alone published. Fact stores, temporal graphs and paging are on Agent memory layers; what to keep in the window on Context engineering.

Go deeper: the Agentic lab runs no retrieval, a single-shot pipeline, a ReAct loop, query decomposition and long context on the 200 HotpotQA questions with Qwen3 1.7B and 4B, with tokens, searches and seconds per question; the Agentic retrieval, long context and memory child takes each further.

8. Production: latency, freshness, tenants, cost, caching

Latency: time the whole request, not the stages. Measured one at a time, the stages of a SciFact request look cheap except the generator. Measured as one request in one process on the same laptop, the embedding and reranking stages are several times slower, because the embedding model, the reranker and the generator share one GPU.

One request, measured two ways

Median milliseconds per query, batch 1, Apple M1 Pro (MPS for the encoders, Metal llama.cpp for Qwen3-1.7B), bench lock held measured. Stages: Qwen3-Embedding query embedding, exact search over 5,183 vectors, ms-marco MiniLM cross-encoder on the top 30, generator time to first token. "On its own": the Pipeline lab's stage timings (40 claims × 3) and the production child's time to first token at about 1,720 prompt tokens. "One process": the production child's end-to-end run (40 claims × 3, 1,644 prompt tokens with the top 5).

The ratios transfer to a server (the reranker and generator dominate, vector search over thousands of documents is negligible); the milliseconds do not (a datacenter GPU is much faster and batches many users). The lesson that transfers exactly: a latency budget is checked on the whole request path, under the real sharing of hardware.

Freshness and re-indexing. New documents must be parsed, chunked, embedded and written to both indexes; deletions must really delete. A model change re-embeds the whole corpus, and the vectors of two models cannot share an index even at the same dimension: halfway through a backfill from MiniLM to bge-small in one index, nDCG@10 falls to 0.374 to 0.379 from 0.645 and 0.713; a bge-small query against an all-MiniLM index scores 0.137 measured, production child. Build the new index beside the old one, then switch. How documents are chunked decides how much a revision costs: on ten revised arXiv papers whose revisions changed 15.0% of the words, fixed 200-word windows re-embedded 75.8% of the words and structure-aware chunks 49.2%, because one inserted word shifts every later fixed window (the Document ingestion child) measured.

Tenants and access control. Filter at retrieval, by tenant and permission, inside the search (sections 1 and 4). Even then, check the engine: in pgvector with row-level security no forbidden row ever came back, but with psycopg's default prepared statements PostgreSQL reused one generic HNSW plan across users, so a user allowed 2.1% of the corpus got 0.96 rows of 10 on average and nothing at all for 123 of 300 claims measured, production child.

Cost per query. The production child's worked example with list prices read on 2026-10-14 (1 million queries a month, a hosted embedder, a hosted reranker on 30 candidates, a small hosted generator reading 5 chunks): $0.0012 per query, of which generation 62% and reranking 36%; the hosted reranker costs more than half as much as the generator because it reads 30 passages where the generator reads 5 derived from vendor prices. The vector store's own bill (read units, replicas, minimums) sits mostly outside that formula. Its Cost calculator has every knob.

Caching. Three caches, three different risks. A prompt (prefix) cache keeps the model's state for a repeated prompt prefix: for a 3,606-token prefix the 1.7 B model's first call took 4,149 ms and later calls 73 ms measured; safe and large. A result cache keyed on the query vector returns a previous query's retrieved list for a near-identical query: at a cosine threshold of 0.90 SciFact's nDCG@10 moved from 0.700 to 0.702, harmless. A semantic answer cache returns a previous query's answer, and near-duplicates with opposite meanings break it: SciFact contains 303 pairs of claims about the same abstract with opposite verdicts, whose median cosine (0.947, Qwen3-Embedding) is higher than that of same-verdict pairs (0.781); replayed at a threshold of 0.95, 144 of the 254 cache hits (57%) would have returned the answer to the opposite claim measured, production child.

Go deeper: RAG in production (latency waterfall, cost calculator, access lab, cache lab, monitoring); prefix caching and serving the generator on Topic: inference-and-serving.

9. The tools

A retrieval system is a stack of separate choices: a parser, a framework or your own code to chunk and wire the steps, an embedding model, an ANN index inside a vector store (or a library such as FAISS), a keyword engine, a reranker, and an evaluation tool. The Tool map is a dated atlas of each layer (owner, licence, latest release, status, the algorithm it actually runs, when to choose it), a "which store" chooser and a timeline. Its measured lesson: the defaults differ more than the algorithms. Given the same SciFact bge-small vectors and nothing changed, hnswlib (ef 10) returns 0.876 of the exact top 10, FAISS IVF (nprobe 1) 0.420, LanceDB's default IVF_PQ index about 0.59, Chroma 0.996 to 0.998, and Qdrant's local mode and Milvus Lite 1.000 because they never build an index; one knob each recovers nearly everything measured, Tool map. Framework defaults bite the same way: LlamaIndex returns 2 chunks unless told otherwise, LangChain's text splitter cuts 4,000 characters (MiniLM reads only its first 256 tokens, a third of such a chunk).

Which to use, in one line each (status and evidence on the Tool map): pgvector when the data already lives in PostgreSQL and fits one server; Qdrant, Weaviate or Milvus as dedicated engines with in-graph filtering and built-in hybrid search; Elasticsearch or OpenSearch when BM25 is already there; FAISS as a library for experiments and exact baselines; a managed service when nobody can operate a database. For models, shortlist open ones you can measure locally (Qwen3-Embedding, bge, gte) against hosted ones (OpenAI, Gemini, Voyage, Cohere) on your own golden set. For evaluation, ranx or pytrec_eval for retrieval metrics; RAGAS, DeepEval or TruLens for judged ones, by way of the RAG and retrieval evaluation page.

Common mistakes

Tuning the generator when the evidence never arrived
A better model or prompt moves only g. Check first whether the evidence was in the prompt; if not, nothing downstream can find it. And the reverse: on the measured SciFact run the search was fine and the generator lost 82 of 92 failures (section 6).
Reporting one end-to-end number
It cannot say which stage failed. Report r, p and g, and a confusion of labels: the 1.7 B model's 0 correct CONTRADICT answers were invisible in "51% accuracy".
Assuming hybrid search always helps
Equal-weight RRF lifted models close to BM25 and hurt the two clearly stronger ones (gte-modernbert 0.767 to 0.763, ColBERT-small 0.743 to 0.731). Measure; weight the stronger retriever, with the weight chosen on held-out queries.
Adding a reranker without checking it beats the first stage
The 22 M MiniLM cross-encoder pulls the fused SciFact list from 0.724 to 0.689 at K 100; Qwen3-Reranker lifts it to 0.782 at K 20. And no reranker can rescue a passage outside its K.
Comparing chunkers at a fixed number of chunks
Bigger chunks send more text, so they win at a fixed k almost by definition. Compare at an equal token budget, where 512-token windows lose to paragraph-aware chunks (45.9% against 64.5%).
Confusing ANN recall with retrieval recall
An index can return 100% of the exact top 10 while the system finds only 84.5% of the labelled abstracts. Tune the index on the first, judge the system on the second.
Dot product on vectors the model did not normalise; one threshold for every model
gte-modernbert loses 0.027 nDCG@10 on SciFact with a raw dot product. Cosine ranges differ by model (bge-small random pairs near 0.56, MiniLM near 0.10): tune thresholds per model.
Binary quantization without rescoring; truncating a model not trained for it
Binary codes alone keep 67% of Qwen3's exact top 10; rescoring 100 restores 99%. int8 with a float query is nearly free. Halving bge-small's dimensions loses 6%, a quarter 19%.
Filtering after the search, or enforcing access in the prompt
A post-filter at 10% visibility returns 1.73 results of 10; a rule in the system prompt leaked the restricted fact in 17 of 18 answers. Filter inside the search, at retrieval.
Benchmarking a store that never used its index
Qdrant's server scans exactly below its 10,000 KB thresholds; Milvus Lite and Qdrant's local mode always scan. Test at production size, on the server you will run.
Timing stages in isolation
Embedding took 49 ms alone and 428 ms inside the full request on a shared GPU. Time the whole path.
A semantic answer cache on near-duplicate questions
Claims that differ by one word can have opposite answers and higher cosine than paraphrases; 57% of cache hits at 0.95 returned the opposite claim's answer.
Tuning anything on the test set, including the prompt
Fusion weights, rerank depth and the answer prompt are knobs; choose them on a tuning split, report the test once. The first SciFact prompt scored 23 of 188 with gold abstracts; the one chosen on training claims 112.
"Long context killed RAG", "agents are always better", "GraphRAG is better RAG"
Each answers a class of question the pipeline cannot, at a price (section 7). Measured on two-hop questions with Qwen3-4B: the agent loop gains 0.084 F1 for 3 times the tokens, a fixed decomposition gains nothing (0.488 against 0.490), and an 8,000-token window of mostly distractors scores below a single search (0.475). For lookups over a large corpus, hybrid search with a reranker is still the cheapest and best measured.

Interview questions, short answers

Explain RAG in two minutes, and why not just fine-tune?
Retrieve the passages that bear on a question from an external corpus, put them in the prompt, have the model answer from them and cite them. Fine-tuning changes how a model behaves but is a poor way to add facts: it cannot be updated per document, cannot cite, cannot give two users different views, and still hallucinates on what it saw once. RAG updates by re-indexing, cites by construction and enforces access at retrieval. They combine: fine-tune for format and domain style, retrieve for facts.
BM25 or embeddings?
Both, usually. BM25 wins on exact identifiers, rare names and domain terms and costs no model; embeddings win on paraphrase. Fuse them with RRF, then check on your data: fusion helped every model close to BM25 on SciFact and hurt the two that clearly beat it. If one dominates, weight it, with the weight chosen on held-out queries.
How is an embedding model trained?
Contrastively, on (query, relevant passage) pairs: InfoNCE asks each query to pick its passage out of a line-up of the batch's other passages (in-batch negatives, free) and mined hard negatives (passages that look relevant but are not). Large batches and hard negatives make the line-up harder; false negatives (unlabelled relevant passages) must be filtered. Often followed by Matryoshka training, instruction prefixes and distillation from a cross-encoder.
HNSW, IVF or exact search?
Exact below about a million vectors if the scan fits the latency budget (one core scans about 37 GB/s here: 112 ms per million 1,024-dim vectors), and always as the ground truth. HNSW for low latency at high recall in memory (knobs M, efSearch). IVF or IVF-PQ when memory or build time dominate (knobs nprobe, m, rescoring). DiskANN when the vectors outgrow RAM. Report ANN recall at the setting, never speed alone.
Our vector search has 0.98 recall but answers are bad. Where do you look?
0.98 is ANN recall against exact search: the index is fine. Measure retrieval recall@K and nDCG on labelled queries with exact search: if low, the embedding model, chunking or query (prefix, domain) is the problem. Then check whether the evidence reaches the prompt (ranking) and whether the model uses it (generation).
Users say the answers are wrong. How do you find the broken stage?
Build a golden set (a few hundred real questions with labelled passages). Log the first stage's top K, the reranked top k and the answer for each. Count the three buckets: evidence not in top K (retrieval), in K not in k (ranking), in the prompt but wrong (generation). Run an oracle prompt with only the gold passages for the ceiling of g. Fix the biggest bucket; on SciFact with a 1.7 B model that was generation, 82 of 92.
How deep should the reranker read?
Sweep K on the golden set against latency. The first stage's recall@K is the ceiling; past the point where it flattens, more K costs linearly more time and gives a reranker more chances to promote a wrong passage. On SciFact the strong rerankers peaked at K 20; the weak one got worse with every extra candidate.
When would you use an agent loop instead of a pipeline? GraphRAG? Long context?
A loop for multi-hop and exploratory questions, whose second search depends on what the first found, with a step budget, since input tokens grow with n(n + 1)/2; a router in front sends lookups to the pipeline. GraphRAG for corpus-global questions ("main themes across everything") when the corpus is stable and the indexing budget is there. Long context when a small corpus fits the window and is read once or holistically; retrieval for scale, cost per query, latency and per-user access.
How do you enforce multi-tenant access control?
Metadata on every chunk at index time (tenant, groups); the filter applied inside each search (BM25 query and ANN traversal), never on the result list and never as a prompt instruction (17 of 18 answers leaked that way here). Then test it: restrictive filters with graph indexes, the engine's planner, prepared-statement plans, and deletion that really deletes.
Design a RAG system: question answering over 5 million internal documents (PDFs, wiki pages, tickets) for 20,000 employees, permission-aware, p95 under 3 s. Walk through it end to end.

1. Clarify and measure first. Question types (lookups, multi-hop, "summarise everything about X"), freshness needs, languages, the permission model, query volume (say 50,000 a day), budget. Build a golden set of 300 to 500 real questions with labelled passages from search logs and tickets, split into tuning and test.

2. Ingestion. A layout-aware parser for PDFs (tables and headings kept), connectors for the wiki and tickets; chunk by structure (sections, then paragraphs, capped near 256 to 512 tokens), title and section path prepended; metadata on every chunk: source, date, owner, access groups, document id and version. Content hashes per chunk so a revision re-embeds only what changed.

3. Indexes. About 5 M documents may be 50 to 100 M chunks: at 1,024 dims float32 that is 200 to 400 GB of vectors, so a Matryoshka model cut to 512 dims with int8 storage (about 26 to 51 GB) plus float originals on disk for rescoring, in an HNSW index sharded across a few nodes; or IVF-PQ if memory is tight. BM25 index on the same chunks. Choose the embedding model by nDCG@10 on the tuning split (open models measured locally against one or two hosted ones).

4. Query path. Conversational rewrite in chat; BM25 and dense search in parallel with the user's access groups as a filter inside each search (top 100 each); RRF, or a weighted fusion tuned on the tuning split; a cross-encoder on the top 20 to 50 (measure K); the top 5 to 8 chunks with ids into the prompt; the generator answers with citations or says it cannot find it.

5. Latency budget (an illustrative split of p95 3 s to first token, to be checked by measurement): rewrite 300 ms (skip when the question stands alone), embed 30 ms on a GPU, search 50 ms, rerank 200 to 400 ms on a GPU at K 30, generator time to first token about 1 s; stream the answer. Time it as one request on the real hardware.

6. Hard parts. Permissions change: sync groups into chunk metadata and filter at query time, never cache answers across users. Freshness: incremental re-index on change events, deletes propagated. Model upgrade: build a new index beside the old, switch when complete. Cost: estimate per query (reranker plus generator dominate) and cache prefixes, not answers.

7. Evaluate and monitor. Offline: recall@K at the rerank depth, nDCG@10, r, p and g, faithfulness by a calibrated judge. Online: citation clicks, "no answer" rate, sampled human review, alerts when retrieval scores drift. Add an agent loop and a router later, only if the golden set shows multi-hop failures the pipeline cannot fix.

Reading tab: every measured number comes from the other tabs of this page or from its child pages, built on the running example in October 2026 on an Apple M1 Pro; the tab's data file is generated from their recorded results (src/read/make_data.py), and the old version of this page and its four old children are saved verbatim in src/read/old/, with each claim checked in src/read/coverage.md.

Pipeline lab

Every stage of a retrieval pipeline, measured on the same running example: how the documents are cut into chunks, how the first stage finds candidates (BM25, embeddings, or both fused), filters, query rewriting, reranking, and finally where a correct answer gets lost between the corpus and the generator's reply.

The running example
SciFact (5,183 scientific abstracts, 300 test claims, each with the abstracts annotators marked relevant), NFCorpus (3,633 medical documents, 323 test queries with graded labels) and, for chunking, QASPER (281 NLP papers, 892 questions whose evidence paragraphs annotators marked). Open models only, all run on one laptop: BM25 (bm25s), four embedding models, three rerankers and Qwen3-1.7B as the generator. Every number marked measured was produced here, on an Apple M1 Pro, in October 2026; published numbers come from the paper or vendor named beside them; constructed marks an input written for this page. The definitions (BM25, embeddings, nDCG, recall@K) are in the Reading tab; the vector indexes are in the Vector search lab.

One claim, end to end

A pipeline is a funnel. The first stage looks at all 5,183 abstracts and keeps about a hundred candidates; a reranker reads the best few dozen of those closely and reorders them; only the top k (here 3) reach the generator's prompt. A relevant abstract that drops out at any stage is gone for good: the generator never sees it. Watch one real SciFact claim go through, then switch the pipeline and run the same claim again.

Claim

Lists are the real top 10 of each stage for this claim (titles shortened); the green row is the abstract the SciFact annotators marked as evidence. Scores: BM25 score, cosine similarity, RRF score, reranker score (a logit, only its order matters). measured

Chunking: where the evidence lands

The problem. A paper is thousands of tokens; an embedding model reads a few hundred at a time, and the prompt can hold only a few passages. So documents are cut into chunks, each indexed on its own. If a cut falls through the middle of the paragraph that answers the question, no chunk holds the whole answer, and the half that does match may rank low.

How it is measured here. QASPER's 892 questions come with the paragraphs annotators used as evidence, located as character spans in the paper. For each strategy: how many chunks it makes, how big; for how many questions an evidence paragraph sits wholly inside one chunk ("intact"); and whether retrieval inside the question's own paper hands the generator text covering at least 90% of an evidence paragraph. Two fair ways to hand text over: the top k chunks, or a token budget filled in rank order. Sizes are in Qwen3 tokens.

Explorer: Zampieri et al. 2019, Predicting the Type and Target of Offensive Posts in Social Media (arXiv 1902.09666, QASPER text). Shaded bands are chunks (alternating colours, purple where two chunks overlap); badges mark where each chunk starts (#1 c7 = BM25's first pick); the green underline is the annotated evidence for the selected question.

Predict: retrieving the top 3 chunks, which wins, 512-token fixed chunks or paragraph-aware chunks of at most 256 tokens? And with a fixed budget of 1,024 tokens?
At the top 3, 512-token chunks win with BM25 (61.4% of questions against 45.3%): three chunks of 512 tokens are about three times the text. At an equal budget of 1,024 tokens the order flips: 45.9% for 512-token chunks against 64.5% for paragraph-aware chunks. Comparing chunkers at a fixed k rewards whoever sends more text.
All 892 questions: share of questions whose evidence the retrieved chunks cover. measured
