The full table
Context written by the generator ("contextual retrieval")

Anthropic's recipe (September 2024): before indexing, a model reads the whole document and writes one or two sentences situating each chunk, which are prepended to the chunk. Their reported result, with Claude 3 Haiku writing the context and their own datasets: the top-20 retrieval failure rate fell from 5.7% to 3.7% with contextual embeddings, 2.9% adding contextual BM25, 1.9% adding a reranker published, vendor.

Run here with Qwen3-1.7B writing the context, Anthropic's prompt verbatim, on 71 papers (every fourth; 1,664 default chunks, 239 questions): 2,560 s of generation, 0.87 M new prompt tokens because llama.cpp kept each paper in its cache (11.1 M without that cache). Result, same papers and questions without and with the context: bge-small top 3 46.9% to 49.4%, but at a 1,024-token budget 57.7% to 55.2%; BM25 top 3 38.5% to 40.2%, budget 49.0% to 48.1% measured. With 239 questions a difference of 2 to 3 points is within noise: a 1.7 B writer gives no clear gain on this task, and some of its "contexts" just repeat the chunk's first lines. Note the setting differs from Anthropic's: here retrieval runs inside one paper, where every chunk shares the same document context.

What the numbers say
  • Cut where the author did. Fixed 256-token windows keep an evidence paragraph whole for 607 of 892 questions (68.0%); splitting on blank lines first (the recursive rule) keeps 838 (93.9%), packing paragraphs within sections 832 (93.3%). At a 1,024-token budget with bge-small, that is 56.8% of questions found for fixed windows against 67.9% (recursive) and 70.0% (paragraphs within sections). The 0.6 B Qwen3-Embedding shows the same gap (59.4% against 70.3%): a bigger embedder does not repair a bad cut.
  • Overlap is a patch, not a fix: 32 tokens of overlap move fixed windows from 546 to 607 intact questions and cost 14% more tokens to index.
  • Compare at equal tokens. Big chunks win at a fixed k because they send more text: semantic chunking at LangChain's default (cut at the 95th percentile of sentence-to-sentence distance) makes chunks of median 342 and up to 4,967 tokens, tops the top-3 chart with BM25 (71.6%), and comes last at a 1,024-token budget (38.6%). Cutting at the 80th percentile gives small chunks that split the evidence (547 intact).
  • Sentence packing ignores paragraphs and does no better than fixed windows (593 intact).
  • A title and section prefix (no model) helps paragraph-aware chunks (bge-small at 1,024 tokens: 70.0% to 72.0%) and not fixed windows (56.8% to 54.9%), whose section label can be wrong for half the window.
  • One caution: QASPER's evidence unit is the paragraph, so "one paragraph per chunk" (median 89 tokens, 888 of 892 intact, 77.5% at 1,024 tokens with bge-small) is favoured by construction. On documents whose answers span paragraphs, packing paragraphs up to a size is the safer default.

BM25, dense, and hybrid

The problem. BM25 matches words: it finds "PPM1D" when the claim says "PPM1D", and misses an abstract that says the same thing in other words. A dense retriever matches meaning: it finds the paraphrase, and can rank a topically similar abstract above the one with the exact gene name. Their mistakes are different, so running both and merging the two lists (hybrid search) often beats either. How BM25's inverted index and a vector index sit inside a database is on Search and vector databases; the defaults each framework ships with are in the Tool map's defaults section (LlamaIndex returns only 2 chunks unless told otherwise).

How the lists are merged. The two scores live on different scales (a BM25 score of 4.45 against a cosine of 0.71), so they cannot simply be added. Two families:

  • Reciprocal rank fusion (RRF) ignores scores and uses ranks: score(d) = Σlists 1 / (k + rank(d)), with k = 60 in the paper that proposed it (Cormack, Clarke and Büttcher, SIGIR 2009) and in most libraries. No tuning, no calibration.
  • Score fusion normalises each list's scores (min-max to [0, 1], or z-score: subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) and takes a weighted sum, α · dense + (1 − α) · BM25. It keeps how much better the first hit is than the second, but α must be chosen, and choosing it on the test set is a leak.

RRF: does k matter?
Score fusion: the weight α, swept on the test set

Each first stage contributes its recorded top 100; a document missing from one list adds 0 to RRF and that list's lowest normalised score to score fusion; the fused list is cut to 100. measured

What the numbers say
  • Hybrid helps a dense model that is about as good as BM25 and disagrees with it. On SciFact, RRF lifts MiniLM-L6 from 0.645 to 0.713 nDCG@10 and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B from 0.700 to 0.724 (better on 69 claims, worse on 50).
  • It can hurt a dense model that is clearly better. gte-modernbert (0.767) drops to 0.763 with RRF k 60, ColBERT-small (0.743) to 0.731: equal-weight fusion gives BM25's weaker list the same say.
  • k barely matters (0.724 to 0.732 for Qwen3 across k from 1 to 1,000), which is why 60 is a safe default.
  • Weighted score fusion beats RRF when its weight is learned on other queries. With α chosen on SciFact's 809 training claims (0.6), z-score fusion scores 0.739 for Qwen3 on the test claims; the best α picked on the test set itself would claim 0.744, a 0.005 leak. On NFCorpus, RRF adds nothing to Qwen3 (0.363 to 0.361) while z-score with α tuned on the dev split gives 0.375.
Tuned on a held-out split, scored on test (nDCG@10)

The knob (RRF k, or α) is the value with the best nDCG@10 on SciFact train (809 claims) or NFCorpus dev; ties go to the value nearest the default. BM25 and dense runs for those splits are computed here with the same settings as the recorded test runs (BM25 reproduces the recorded test top 10 for every query).

RRF calculator, on real lists

Pick a claim and move k. The table is the fused top 10 of the real BM25 and Qwen3-Embedding top 30 lists (fused here over the top 30 of each, so ranks past 30 count as absent). The first three claims are rescued by fusion; the last two are hurt by it.

Small k makes the very top of each list dominate (rank 1 scores 1/2 at k = 1, rank 10 scores 1/11); large k flattens the curve, so being in both lists matters more than being first in one.

Filters: inside the search or after it

The problem. Real queries come with conditions: only this customer's documents, only what this user may read, only papers after 2020. A metadata filter can run inside the search (only allowed documents compete: a pre-filter) or after it (fetch the top N from everything, then drop what is not allowed: a post-filter). The post-filter is easy to bolt on and silently returns fewer results, sometimes none, when the filter is selective.

The setup. SciFact has no access metadata, so an attribute is constructed: each abstract gets an access group, crc32(document id) mod G, so a user sees 1/G of the corpus; each claim is asked by a user of its evidence abstract's group (the answer is always allowed). Exact search with Qwen3-Embedding, so the only difference is where the filter runs; how filters interact with approximate indexes such as HNSW is in the Vector search lab.

Results returned, of 10 asked, by filter selectivity

300 SciFact test claims, Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B, exact inner-product search. measured

What the numbers say
  • When a user may see 10% of the corpus, fetching 10 and filtering returns 1.73 results on average, and nothing at all for 14 of 300 claims. The evidence reaches the results for 255 claims, against 284 when the filter runs inside the search.
  • Over-fetching repairs it only partly: with the top 100 fetched, the evidence is found as often as with the pre-filter (284), but 96 claims still get fewer than 10 results. At 1% visibility even 1,000 fetched leaves 112 claims short.
  • The pre-filter always returns 10. Its evidence count even rises as the filter narrows (284 at 10%, 299 at 1%, against 256 unfiltered), but that is the construction: the evidence is always allowed and fewer abstracts compete with it.
Why vector stores make this hard, briefly
With an exact scan the pre-filter is free: skip disallowed rows. With an approximate index (HNSW, IVF) the graph or clusters were built over every document, so a restrictive filter can cut the paths the search walks, and engines add workarounds: iterative index scans that keep fetching until enough rows pass (pgvector since 0.8.0), filter-aware graph traversal (ACORN, Weaviate's default since v1.34), or a brute-force scan when few rows pass. The Tool map lists which engine does what; the Vector search lab measures filtered HNSW.

Rewriting the query

The problem. The words a user types are not always the words of the documents. Three fixes, each run here with the local generator (Qwen3-1.7B, greedy):

  • HyDE (Gao et al. 2022, "Precise Zero-Shot Dense Retrieval without Relevance Labels"): ask the model to write a fake answer passage, embed that instead of the question, since a passage looks more like the documents than a question does. The prompt is the authors' SciFact prompt from their code (texttron/hyde, promptor.py): "Please write a scientific paper passage to support/refute the claim."
  • Multi-query: ask for three rewordings, retrieve with each and the original, fuse the four lists with RRF.
  • Conversational rewrite: in a chat, "does it help?" means nothing without the earlier turns; the model rewrites the last message into a standalone query.
HyDE and multi-query on the 300 SciFact test claims measured
What the numbers say
  • HyDE helps a little, and how to use it depends on the retriever. For Qwen3-Embedding the fake passage alone lifts nDCG@10 from 0.700 to 0.718; for bge-small the passage alone hurts (0.692) and only the passage averaged with the claim helps (0.733, from 0.713). For BM25, appending the passage to the claim adds words the abstracts use: recall@100 rises from 0.913 to 0.943.
  • Multi-query buys almost nothing here (Qwen3: 0.699 against 0.700, better on 36 claims and worse on 36): SciFact claims are already specific, and the rewordings mostly repeat them.
  • Both cost a generator call before retrieval can start: about 2.2 s per claim for HyDE and 0.8 s for the three rewordings with the 1.7 B model on this laptop, under heavy load from other jobs. That is more than the whole retrieval stage.
Eight follow-up questions constructed: two-turn chats written for this page from SciFact test claims, so that the second turn leans on the first. The cells give the rank of the claim's evidence abstract when retrieving with the follow-up alone, the whole chat pasted together, the generator's rewrite, and (for reference) the original claim.

With the follow-up alone, the evidence lands in the top 3 for 3 (bge-small) to 5 (Qwen3-Embedding) of the 8 chats; with the generator's rewrite, for 6 to 7 of 8, as often as when the whole two-turn chat is pasted in. One rewrite (the mitochondria chat) turned the question into a general one and did worse than the follow-up alone. Longer chats, where pasting everything dilutes the query, were not tested.

Reranking: how deep, and with what

The problem. A first-stage retriever must score millions of documents in milliseconds, so it compares a query vector with precomputed document vectors (or word statistics) and never reads the two texts together. A cross-encoder reranker does read them together: query and candidate go through one transformer and come out as one relevance score. That is far more accurate and far too slow for the whole corpus, so it reads only the first stage's top K.

The two questions. How deep (K: more candidates means more chances to rescue the evidence, and more latency)? And which model: a reranker only helps when it is better than the first stage it reorders.

First stage

SciFact, 300 test claims. The reranked top K come first, then the first stage's ranks K+1 onward unchanged. measured

What the numbers say
  • A strong reranker is the biggest single gain in the pipeline. Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B on the hybrid top 20 lifts nDCG@10 from 0.724 to 0.782 and recall@10 from 0.862 to 0.902; bge-reranker-v2-m3 reaches 0.757.
  • Deeper is not always better. Both large rerankers peak at K 20 on the hybrid list (0.782 and 0.757) and slip at K 30 and 50 (0.778 and 0.779; 0.749 and 0.746), although the first stage's recall rises from 0.912 to 0.936: each extra candidate is one more chance to promote a wrong abstract above the right one, and the cost grows with every candidate.
  • A weak reranker hurts. The 22 M CE MiniLM (trained on MS MARCO web queries) makes the hybrid list worse the deeper it reads: 0.724 without it, 0.702 at K 30, 0.689 at K 100. It reproduces the BEIR paper's BM25+CE number (0.688) because BM25 alone is weaker than it.
  • The price is time. On this laptop Qwen3-Reranker scores about 5 pairs per second: K 20 costs about 4 seconds per query, which is why the latency section matters.

Limits: the setup scored the two large rerankers only on the BM25 top 30 and the Qwen3-Embedding top 30 (the union), and this tab scored the 2,715 extra pairs the hybrid top 50 needs (Qwen3-Reranker 4.9 pairs/s, bge-reranker-v2-m3 14.1 to 14.3 pairs/s, same settings). K 100 for them (about 12,200 more pairs, roughly 40 minutes for Qwen3-Reranker) was not run, given the flat curve from 20 to 50; CE MiniLM covers K up to 100.

Where the answer gets lost

The idea. An answer can only be right for the right reason if three things happen in a row: the first stage puts the evidence in its top K; the reranker keeps it in the top k that reach the prompt; the generator reads it and answers correctly. So end-to-end accuracy factors as

A = rK × pk|K × g
rK
share of questions whose evidence is in the first stage's top K (recall@K, read as "found at all")
pk|K
of those, the share still in the top k after reranking
g
of those, the share the generator gets right

Each factor has its own fix (better retriever or bigger K; better reranker or bigger k; better generator or prompt), so measuring them apart tells you where to spend. A single accuracy number does not.

The task. SciFact claims, with the original release's labels: given the top k abstracts, the generator answers SUPPORT, CONTRADICT or NOT ENOUGH INFO and cites the abstract it relied on. The check is deterministic, no judge: an answer is correct when the label matches the annotators' and the cited abstract is one they marked as evidence. The decomposition uses the 188 test claims that have evidence (124 SUPPORT, 64 CONTRADICT). Pipeline: hybrid RRF, Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B on the top K, Qwen3-1.7B on the top k.

Reranker
k (abstracts in the prompt)

188 SciFact test claims with annotated evidence; generator Qwen3-1.7B (GGUF Q4_K_M in llama.cpp, greedy, thinking off). measured

What the numbers say (reranker on, K 30, k 3)
  • Retrieval is not the problem here: the hybrid first stage has an evidence abstract in its top 30 for 186 of 188 claims (r = 0.989), and the reranker keeps it in the top 3 for 178 of those (p = 0.957). Only 10 claims are lost before the prompt.
  • The generator is: of the 178 claims with evidence in the prompt, it answers 96 correctly (g = 0.539), so A = 0.511. Even given only the gold abstracts it gets 112 of 188 (0.596): the ceiling for this model and prompt.
  • Why g is low: with abstracts in the prompt, Qwen3-1.7B never once answered CONTRADICT (it did twice in 300 closed-book answers). None of the 64 CONTRADICT claims was answered correctly, and almost all of them reached the prompt, so they are lost at generation; on SUPPORT claims it is right 96 times of 124. A single accuracy number hides this; a confusion of labels shows it at once.
  • The reranker still pays: without it (first stage only, k 3) the evidence reaches the prompt for 171 claims instead of 178, and 90 claims are answered correctly instead of 96.
  • More abstracts are not better for a small model: with the reranker, g falls from 0.626 at k 1 to 0.539 at k 3 and 0.530 at k 5; the extra abstracts distract it.
  • Closed book (no abstracts), the model gets the label right on 45 of 188 claims and can cite nothing.
  • Lucky labels are rare with the citation check: 4 claims get the right label without evidence in the prompt; the check refuses them because the cited abstract is not evidence.
How the answer prompt was chosen (and why it matters)

The first prompt ("does the evidence SUPPORT the claim, CONTRADICT it, or is there NOT ENOUGH INFO") made the 1.7 B model answer NOT ENOUGH INFO almost always: given the gold abstracts it was right on 23 of the 188 test claims. Changing the prompt on the test claims would be tuning on the test set, so three prompts were compared on SciFact train claims, each with its gold abstracts in the prompt (120 claims with evidence, 60 without):

Promptright, claims with evidenceright, claims withoutbalanced
p1: "SUPPORT, CONTRADICT, or NOT ENOUGH INFO?"17 / 12060 / 600.571
p2: "SUPPORT or CONTRADICT? NOT ENOUGH INFO only if no abstract addresses the claim" (chosen)78 / 12041 / 600.667
p3: role, definitions of each label86 / 12011 / 600.450

p2 was then run once on the test claims. Thinking mode (Qwen3's reasoning before answering) was started and stopped: about 8 s per answer here, about 5 hours for the 2,300 answers of this section. The lesson transfers: a prompt is a component of the pipeline with its own failure mode, and is tuned on held-out data like any other knob. measured

Latency: what one query costs

Per-query time of each stage for one user at a time (batch 1), median over 40 SciFact claims and 3 repeats, measured on the Apple M1 Pro under the shared bench lock. measured

What the numbers say
  • Retrieval itself is nearly free at this size: BM25 0.25 ms, exact search over 5,183 vectors 0.51 ms, RRF 0.04 ms. Embedding the query with the 0.6 B Qwen3-Embedding costs 49 ms, a hundred times more.
  • The reranker dominates, and grows linearly with K: CE MiniLM 58 / 155 / 590 ms for K 10 / 30 / 100; bge-reranker-v2-m3 0.84 / 2.18 s for K 10 / 30; Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B 2.49 / 6.62 s. The most accurate reranker here is also 40 times slower than the small one.
  • Generation of a one-line answer from a 1,100-token prompt takes 0.74 s with the 1.7 B model (median of the 2,299 answers in the section above, prompts of median 1,126 tokens read at about 1,040 tokens/s); a long answer costs far more, at about 88 generated tokens per second.
  • What transfers: the order (reranker and generator dominate, the vector search is negligible until the corpus is millions of documents, see the Vector search lab) and the linear growth of rerank cost with K. Not the milliseconds: a datacenter GPU runs these models many times faster, and servers batch many users' queries. Load average during the runs 1.2 to 3.9.

Common mistakes, and interview questions

Comparing chunkers at a fixed number of chunks
Bigger chunks send more text, so they win at a fixed k almost by definition (512-token chunks: 61.4% at the top 3 with BM25). Compare at the same token budget, where they lose (45.9% at 1,024 tokens against 64.5% for paragraph-aware chunks).
Cutting on token counts and ignoring the document's structure
Fixed 256-token windows keep an evidence paragraph intact for 68.0% of QASPER questions; splitting on paragraphs first (the recursive rule, or paragraphs packed within sections) keeps 93.3 to 93.9%. Overlap is a weak patch: 32 tokens of overlap move fixed windows from 61.2% to 68.0%.
Assuming hybrid always helps
Equal-weight RRF helped every model whose quality is close to BM25's and hurt the two that beat BM25 clearly on SciFact (gte-modernbert 0.767 to 0.763, ColBERT-small 0.743 to 0.731). Measure on your data; if one retriever dominates, weight it.
Tuning the fusion weight, k, or the rerank depth on the test set
It looks like progress and is a leak. Hold out queries (SciFact train here) to pick the knob, then report the test score once.
Filtering after the search
With a selective filter the post-filter quietly returns fewer results or none (1.73 of 10 on average at 10% visibility, 14 empty answers of 300). Filter inside the search, or over-fetch and check how many survive.
Adding a reranker without checking it beats the first stage
The 22 M MiniLM cross-encoder trained on MS MARCO adds nothing to Qwen3-Embedding on SciFact (0.700 at K 100) and pulls the hybrid list down as K grows (0.724 to 0.689 at K 100). Qwen3-Reranker-0.6B on the top 30 lifts the same lists to 0.765 (dense) and 0.778 (hybrid).
Reporting one accuracy number
A label can be right without the evidence: on SciFact two thirds of the labelled claims are SUPPORT, so a model that always says SUPPORT scores 66% "accuracy". Check the citation too, and split the failures into retrieval, ranking and generation.

Interview questions, short answers

Users say the RAG system gives wrong answers. How do you find the broken stage?
Build a golden set of questions with the passages that answer them. For each, log the first stage's top K, the reranked top k and the answer. Count: evidence not in top K (retrieval), in K but not in k (ranking), in the prompt but answered wrong (generation). Fix the biggest bucket first; give the generator the gold passages (an oracle run) to get the ceiling of g.
Should we add BM25 to our vector search?
Probably, if queries carry identifiers, rare names or domain terms, and the dense model is not far ahead of BM25 on your data. Start with RRF (k 60, no tuning); if one retriever dominates, use a weighted fusion with the weight chosen on held-out queries. Measure per query wins and losses, not just the mean.
How do you choose a chunk size?
Split on the document's own structure first (sections, paragraphs), then cap the size. Measure on questions with located evidence: share of evidence intact in one chunk, and retrieval at an equal token budget, not at an equal number of chunks. Smaller chunks rank more precisely; bigger chunks carry more context per hit.
How many candidates should the reranker see?
Sweep K on a golden set against latency. The first stage's recall@K is the ceiling: a reranker cannot recover what it is not given. Past the point where recall@K flattens, extra K costs time and gives a weak reranker more chances to promote wrong documents.
Pre-filter or post-filter for access control?
Inside the search (pre-filter), always for access control: a post-filter can return fewer results than asked, or none, and its behaviour depends on how selective the filter is for that user. With an ANN index, check the engine's filtered-search strategy and measure recall with a restrictive filter.
Our reranker made nDCG worse. How is that possible?
It is weaker than the first stage on this domain (a small model trained on web search reordering a strong embedder's list), or it was given a deep list it then reorders badly. Check reranker-alone quality, and sweep K.

How this was measured, and the limits

  • Machine: Apple M1 Pro (8 performance and 2 efficiency cores, 16 GB unified memory), PyTorch MPS and llama.cpp (Metal), October 2026. Shared with other agents: every timing carries its load average in the scripts' records; the ratios between stages transfer to a server, the milliseconds do not (a datacenter GPU runs the encoders and rerankers many times faster, and servers batch concurrent queries).
  • Relevance numbers (nDCG@10, recall) are deterministic: pytrec_eval over the recorded top-100 runs; the same scripts reproduce them exactly. Generator outputs are greedy (temperature 0) and cached by prompt.
  • Running example and baselines: datasets, models, revisions and the baseline table against BEIR and MTEB are defined once for the whole page (the root's src/data/README.md); every baseline here matches it.
  • Scripts: src/pipe/ in the repository (fusion, filters, chunking, query rewriting, reranking, end to end, latency); make_data.py builds everything this tab draws from their outputs.
  • Generator: a 1.7 B model. Its g is far below a frontier model's; the shape (which factor dominates, what a reranker changes) transfers, the absolute accuracy does not.
  • Not run here: see the notes under each section.
Not run here, and why
  • Late chunking (Günther et al. 2024, arXiv 2409.04701: embed the whole document once, then pool the token vectors of each chunk): it needs a long-context embedder trained with mean pooling. The running example's long-context embedders pool differently (gte-modernbert uses the CLS token, Qwen3-Embedding the last token of a causal model), so a late-chunking run would measure a pooling the models were never trained for.
  • Generator-written context on every paper: about 30 s of generation per paper here, so it ran on every fourth paper (71 of 281); the comparison uses the same papers with and without the context.
  • A larger generator: the 4 B model files were missing from the shared model store while this tab's generator runs were scheduled (a temporary-file cleaner had removed them; they were restored later), so every answer here is the 1.7 B model through llama.cpp. A 4 B or frontier model would move g, not r or p.
  • Judged answer quality (faithfulness, groundedness with an LLM judge): SciFact's labels and evidence ids allow an exact check, and judged metrics belong to RAG and retrieval evaluation.
  • Filtered approximate search (HNSW with a restrictive filter): the Vector search lab.

Vector search lab

How text becomes a vector, how two vectors are compared, which embedding model to use, how to make vectors smaller, and how an index finds the nearest ones without comparing against all of them. Everything is measured on the same running example as the rest of this page.

The running example
SciFact (5,183 scientific abstracts, 300 test claims, each with the abstracts annotators marked relevant), embedded by four open models whose vectors the setup computed once: all-MiniLM-L6-v2, bge-small-en-v1.5, gte-modernbert-base and Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B. Every number marked measured was produced on an Apple M1 Pro in October 2026; published numbers come from the paper or vendor named beside them. Relevance numbers (nDCG, recall) are deterministic; timings are labelled with the load average of a shared machine. The index internals (HNSW and IVF-PQ labs, the full speed and memory frontier, filtered search, DiskANN, code reading of FAISS and hnswlib) live on the child page Vector indexes from the inside; this tab is the overview.
What an embedding isCosine, dot, L2Which modelHow they are trainedSmaller vectorsExact vs approximateThe two recallsSpeed, memory, recallMistakes and interview questionsMethod and limits

What an embedding is

The problem. BM25 matches words. A claim such as "Mitochondria are uninvolved in apoptosis" should also find an abstract that says, for example, "cytochrome c release triggers programmed cell death", which shares almost no words with it. We need a representation of meaning that can be compared quickly.

How it works. An embedding model is a neural network that reads a text and outputs a fixed list of numbers, a vector (Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B outputs 1,024 numbers; bge-small 384). It is trained so that texts which answer each other land close together and unrelated texts land far apart (how: How they are trained, below). Each number on its own means nothing; only distances between vectors carry information. Retrieval with embeddings is then geometry: embed every document once, embed the query, return the documents whose vectors are nearest. This is called dense retrieval (every one of the 1,024 numbers is used), as opposed to BM25's sparse vectors (one slot per vocabulary word, almost all zero).

Seeing it. Nobody can look at 1,024 dimensions, so the map below squeezes real Qwen3-Embedding vectors into 2. That squeeze always loses information, and the two common ways of doing it lose different things. Each dot is one real text from the four corpora of the running example; the six large dots in the text colour are SciFact test claims embedded as queries (the selected one has a blue ring). Pick a claim: its 10 true nearest abstracts (by cosine in 1,024 dimensions, over all 5,183) get a ring, the abstract annotators marked relevant is green.

Predict: on the PCA map, how many of the claim's 10 true nearest abstracts are among the 10 dots closest to it?
What the picture can and cannot tell you
Use a 2-D map to see that topics cluster and to spot a corpus that sits apart; never to judge whether retrieval works. Retrieval is decided in the full 1,024 dimensions, and the numbers in the next sections are measured there.

Cosine, dot product, L2: comparing two vectors

The problem. "Nearest" needs a definition. Three are in common use, every vector database asks you to pick one, and picking the wrong one is silent: the search still returns ten results.

dot(q, d) = Σi qi di    cos(q, d) = dot(q, d) / (|q| |d|)    L2(q, d) = |q − d|
|q|
the length (norm) of q, √Σ qi2
dot
larger is closer; grows with the lengths of both vectors
cos
larger is closer; only the angle counts (from −1 to 1)
L2
smaller is closer; |q − d|2 = |q|2 + |d|2 − 2 dot(q, d)

Why normalising makes them agree. If every vector has length 1, then cos = dot and |q − d|2 = 2 − 2 cos, so all three put the documents in the same order. Most embedding models normalise their output (three of the four here have a Normalize step in their sentence-transformers configuration), and the setup stored all four normalised, which is why every other section of this page can use the dot product as cosine. The engine-side view of the same identity, and the pgvector operators for each metric, are on Search and vector databases.

When they disagree. gte-modernbert-base has no Normalize step: encode() returns vectors of different lengths. Below, the SciFact corpus and the 300 claims were embedded again without normalising, and ranked three ways. Toggle "normalise" to see the three lists become one.

Cosine values are not comparable across models

Which embedding model: quality, size, speed

The problem. Leaderboards rank hundreds of models on averages over dozens of tasks. What matters is your corpus, your queries, your latency budget and your memory. The four models below span the common choices: a 22 M-parameter tutorial model, a 33 M classic, a 149 M modern encoder, and a 0.6 B decoder turned embedder.

How to read it. Quality is nDCG@10 (how high the relevant abstracts sit in the top 10; 1 is perfect) and recall@100 (share of relevant abstracts anywhere in the top 100) on the test queries. Size is what the index stores per document (dims × 4 bytes as float32) and the model's weights. Speed is documents per second when indexing (paid once per corpus) and milliseconds per query (paid on every request). Pick a column for the bars.

Predict: which model ranks SciFact best?
What transfers
The ordering of these four is a fact about SciFact and NFCorpus, not about the models: on HotpotQA the order changes again (bge-small 0.860 nDCG@10, gte 0.857, Qwen3 0.825 on the multi-hop set of the running example), and Qwen3-Embedding declares HotpotQA and FEVER among its training data, so it is not zero-shot there (Tool map, MTEB notes). The ratios of cost transfer better: per document, the 0.6 B decoder costs about 20 times a 33 M encoder here (6.4 against 144 documents per second), roughly in proportion to its parameter count (18 times), which holds on any hardware. Absolute milliseconds do not transfer: a server GPU is much faster and batches concurrent queries (not run here). The leaderboard view, and the published scores of hosted models, are in the Tool map.

How embedding models are trained: contrastive learning from zero

The problem. A language model already turns text into vectors (its hidden states), but nothing in next-token training asks a claim and the abstract that supports it to end up close. Averaging those raw states gives poor retrieval. The geometry has to be taught.

The data: pairs. Training needs many (query, positive) pairs: a question and its answer passage, a title and its body, a search query and the page users clicked, a claim and its evidence. Modern recipes add pairs written by a language model. Qwen3-Embedding, for example, reports about 150 million synthetic pairs for a first weakly supervised stage, then about 12 million selected synthetic pairs plus labelled data for supervised fine-tuning, then merging checkpoints (Qwen3 Embedding report, sections 3.2 and 3.3; vendor).

The loss: pick your positive out of a line-up. For each query in a batch, compute its cosine with every candidate document; divide by a temperature τ; apply a softmax; the loss is minus the log-probability of the true positive. This is InfoNCE, a cross-entropy where the "classes" are the candidates. Pushing that probability up pulls the positive closer and pushes the others away.

Li = − log   exp(cos(qi, di+) / τ)  /  Σj exp(cos(qi, dj) / τ)
di+
the positive of query i
dj
every candidate in the line-up: the positive, the other queries' positives (in-batch negatives) and any hard negatives
τ
temperature: small τ sharpens the softmax so small cosine gaps matter (SimCSE settled on τ = 0.05, Gao et al. 2021, appendix D)

In-batch negatives are free. The other pairs in the batch already have their documents embedded, so every query gets B − 1 negatives at no extra cost (the trick of DPR, Karpukhin et al. 2020, and SimCSE). Bigger batches mean more negatives, and more chance that one of them is close: BGE's general-purpose stage used batches as large as 19,200 and relied on in-batch negatives alone (C-Pack paper, section 3.4).

Hard negatives teach the fine distinctions. A random abstract about bacteria is an easy negative for a claim about homocysteine. A hard negative is a document that looks relevant but is not, usually mined by running a retriever and taking a high-ranked non-positive. BGE's task-specific stage adds one such negative per pair, "mined from the task's original corpus, following the ANN-style sampling strategy" (same section). The risk is the false negative: the mined document is in fact relevant but was never labelled, and training then pushes a correct answer away.

Seeing it on real vectors. No training runs here. Below is a real batch of 8 SciFact train claims with their labelled abstracts, scored by the already-trained models; the loss is computed live from those cosines. The "hard negative" column is, for each claim, the highest-scoring non-relevant abstract of the whole corpus under the same model. Step through the rows, move τ, and toggle the hard negatives (before/after on the same batch).

Bigger batches are a harder line-up. Over all SciFact train claims in random batches (seed 0): share of claims whose positive already outscores all B − 1 in-batch negatives, and the mean InfoNCE loss at τ 0.05. measured

False negatives are common, not rare

What else goes into a modern recipe (each named once here; the depth belongs to the embedding models child page): instruction prefixes so one model serves several tasks (Qwen3's Instruct: ...\nQuery:, bge's query prefix; measure them, since bge-small's prefix is within noise here, 0.720 without against 0.713 with on SciFact and the reverse on NFCorpus, while Qwen3's instruction is worth 2.1 to 6.6 points); Matryoshka training, which adds the same loss on the first 32, 64, ... dimensions so that truncated vectors still work (next section); distillation from a cross-encoder's scores; and model merging. The general theory of contrastive losses is on Contrastive and self-supervised learning.

Go deeper: a real fine-tune of a small model on the SciFact train split, measured before and after, is on the child page Embedding models: training, choosing and fine-tuning. It is not run here: the root shows the mechanism on real vectors and leaves training to the child.

Smaller vectors: Matryoshka truncation and quantization

The problem. Qwen3-Embedding stores 1,024 float32 numbers per document: 4,096 bytes. SciFact's 5,183 abstracts take 21 MB, but 10 million chunks would take 41 GB of memory before any index structure, and memory is what a vector database bills for. Two independent knobs shrink a vector: keep fewer numbers, or store each number in fewer bits.

Matryoshka truncation (fewer numbers). A model trained with Matryoshka Representation Learning (Kusupati et al. 2022) gets the contrastive loss applied to the first 32, 64, 128, ... dimensions as well as to all of them, so the most useful information is packed at the front, like nested dolls. You keep the first d numbers and re-normalise. A model trained without it can be cut the same way, but nothing promised that the front holds the most. Qwen3-Embedding declares Matryoshka support from 32 to 1,024 dimensions (model card, vendor); bge-small and gte-modernbert do not.

Quantization (fewer bits per number). int8: map each dimension's range onto 256 levels, 1 byte per number (4 times smaller). Binary: keep only the sign of each number, 1 bit (32 times smaller), compared by counting differing bits (Hamming distance). Rescoring repairs most of the damage: retrieve R candidates with the small codes, then re-rank just those R with the full float32 vectors, read from disk or a cheaper tier. Product quantization (PQ), which compresses further by encoding chunks of the vector against learned codebooks, is part of the IVF-PQ lab on the child page.

Explorer: Qwen3-Embedding on SciFact (300 claims). Choose how many dimensions to keep, how to store each, and how many candidates to rescore. "Same as full search" = share of the full float32 1,024-dim top 10 that this setting returns (the index-side recall); nDCG@10 and recall@10 are against the relevance labels. measured

Predict: binary codes of all 1,024 dimensions (128 bytes, 32 times smaller), then rescoring the top 100 with the float vectors. How much nDCG@10 is left of the full 0.700?
Before/after: Matryoshka against plain truncation. nDCG@10 on SciFact as a share of each model's own full-size score, when only the first d dimensions are kept (float32, re-normalised). measured

What transfers
The shapes do: binary codes need rescoring; int8 with a float query loses almost nothing; quantizing the query too changes which documents come back even when the quality score barely moves; truncation hurts a model not trained for it more. The exact numbers are SciFact's (5,183 short abstracts, one relevant abstract per claim for most claims). On a corpus of millions, more near-duplicates compete for the top 10, so compression costs more recall there: check on your own data at your own size. Engines implement these differently (calibration ranges, asymmetric distance, oversampling factors): the Tool map lists which store offers which, and the child page measures them on Quora's 522,931 vectors.

Exact search, and why indexes approximate

Exact (flat) search compares the query with every stored vector and keeps the best k. It is always right and needs no index; its cost grows with the number of vectors times their size. Measured on this laptop on one core, it streams about 37 GB of vectors per second: SciFact's 21 MB takes about half a millisecond per claim, the 522,931 Quora questions (384 dims) 22 ms per query, and 1 million 1,024-dim vectors would take about 112 ms (child page, sections 2 and 12). Below roughly a million vectors, exact search is often fast enough and is the honest baseline.

Approximate nearest neighbour (ANN) indexes look at a small part of the data and accept that they will sometimes miss a true neighbour. Three ideas cover almost every index in use:

IVF: cluster, then search a few clusters

k-means splits the vectors into nlist cells; a query scans only the nprobe cells whose centres are nearest. Misses a neighbour that sits in a cell it did not open. Knob: nprobe.

PQ: compress, then compare codes

Each vector is cut into m chunks and each chunk replaced by the id of its nearest learned centroid, so 4,096 bytes become m bytes. Distances are estimated from the codes; the estimate reorders neighbours. Knobs: m, rescoring.

HNSW: walk a graph

Each vector is linked to a few near neighbours; a query starts somewhere and greedily walks toward closer vectors, keeping a frontier of efSearch candidates. Misses a neighbour the walk never reaches. Knobs: M, efSearch.

IVF-PQ combines the first two (the classic billion-scale design); DiskANN keeps a graph on SSD; filtered search, deletes and updates change all of them. Each is built, animated and measured on Vector indexes from the inside.

Before/after on one claim: the same query vector (Qwen3-Embedding, 1,024 dims) through exact search, HNSW and IVF-PQ, all built with FAISS on the 5,183 SciFact abstracts. Rows move to their new rank; a dashed row is a true top-10 abstract the index did not return; an orange border marks an abstract that was not in the exact top 10. measured

The two recalls

Two different questions share one word. ANN recall@10 asks: of the 10 vectors exact search would return, how many did the index return? It needs no labels, measures only the index, and is what vector database benchmarks report. Retrieval recall@10 asks: of the documents a human marked relevant, how many are in the top 10? It needs labels and measures the whole system: the embedding model first, the index second. An index with ANN recall 1.0 cannot fix a model that puts the answer at rank 40.

Every index setting, the same 300 claims. x: ANN recall@10 against exact search; y: retrieval recall@10 against the labels. The dashed line is what you would get if the index lost relevant abstracts exactly as often as any other neighbour (ceiling × ANN recall). measured
Claim by claim. Each square is one claim. Pick a setting:

Predict: IVF at nprobe 8 returns 90% of the exact top 10. What share of the labelled abstracts does it find, if exact search finds 84.5%?

Speed, memory, recall: the short version

Every index trades three things: how many true neighbours it returns, how many queries per second it serves, and how many bytes it holds per vector (plus build time). The child page measured seven families on SciFact, on four corpora stacked and on BEIR Quora; the Quora sweep is summarised here because only at half a million vectors does exact search become slow. measured by the Vector indexes child, FAISS 1.15.1, one thread, one query at a time, bench lock held.

Go deeper: the full recall, speed and memory frontier with build times, the HNSW build-and-search lab, the IVF-PQ lab with its lookup tables, filtered search (pre-filter, post-filter, in-graph, ACORN), deletes, Vamana and ScaNN, and the FAISS and hnswlib search loops read line by line: Vector indexes from the inside. The engine view (pgvector, Lucene) is on Search and vector databases.

Common mistakes, and interview questions

Using dot product on vectors the model did not normalise
Choosing the embedding model from a leaderboard average
On SciFact the 149 M gte-modernbert beats the 0.6 B Qwen3-Embedding (0.767 against 0.700); on NFCorpus Qwen3 wins (0.363 against 0.343). An average over dozens of tasks hides both. Build a labelled set from your own queries (a few hundred is enough to separate models this far apart) and measure.
Reusing a similarity threshold across models
bge-small puts unrelated pairs near 0.5 and good matches near 0.75; Qwen3-Embedding puts unrelated pairs near 0.2. "Keep results above 0.7" means different things for each, and changes silently when you upgrade the model. Tune thresholds on labelled data, per model.
Mixing vectors from two models in one index
Vectors from different models live in unrelated spaces even when the dimension matches. The production child page measured a half-migrated index (MiniLM to bge-small, both 384-d): nDCG@10 fell to 0.374 to 0.379 from 0.645 and 0.713 (prd, measured). Re-embed everything, then switch.
Truncating a model that was not trained for it
Halving bge-small's 384 dimensions loses 6% of its nDCG on SciFact; a quarter loses 19%. Qwen3-Embedding, trained with Matryoshka, loses 2% at half and 5% at a quarter. Check the model card, then measure.
Binary quantization without rescoring
Sign bits alone keep only 67% of the full top 10 for Qwen3 on SciFact (nDCG 0.680 against 0.700). Rescoring the top 100 with the float vectors brings back 99% of it and the full nDCG. Keep the originals somewhere cheaper and rescore.
Reporting ANN recall as if it were retrieval quality
An index can return 100% of the exact top 10 while the system finds only 84.5% of the relevant abstracts, because the embedding model already ranks the rest below 10. Report both: ANN recall to tune the index, retrieval recall and nDCG to judge the system.
Reading clusters and distances off a 2-D picture
PCA kept 10.5% of the variance of these vectors and placed between 0 and 3 of each claim's 10 true neighbours among its 10 nearest dots; t-SNE kept neighbourhoods but invents the distances between clusters. Use maps to explore, never to evaluate.
Treating mined hard negatives as certainly negative
For about 39% of SciFact train claims an unlabelled abstract outscores the labelled positive. Some are real model errors, some are unlabelled positives. Filter (Qwen3-Embedding masks negatives that score more than 0.1 above the positive) or check a sample by hand before fine-tuning on them.

Interview questions, short answers

What is an embedding, and why does retrieval with it work?
A fixed-length vector a trained network assigns to a text. Contrastive training on (query, relevant text) pairs makes the cosine between a query and its relevant texts larger than with other texts, so nearest-neighbour search in that space returns relevant texts even when they share no words with the query.
Cosine, dot product or L2?
Use what the model was trained with. If vectors are normalised, all three give the same order, and the dot product is cheapest. If not, the dot product favours long vectors and L2 favours short ones; cosine is the safe default. Normalise once at write time.
Explain in-batch negatives and hard negatives.
InfoNCE asks each query to pick its positive among candidates. In-batch negatives reuse the other pairs' documents in the same batch (free; harder as the batch grows). Hard negatives are mined documents that look relevant but are not; they teach fine distinctions but include false negatives, which have to be filtered.
We have 100 million 1,024-dim vectors. How do you fit them in memory?
float32 is 410 GB. Options, combined: a Matryoshka model cut to 256 or 512 dims (measure the loss); int8 (4 times smaller, almost no loss with a float query) or binary codes (32 times smaller) with the float originals on SSD for rescoring the top 100 to 400; or IVF-PQ / DiskANN, which keep compressed codes in memory and full vectors on disk. Measure recall at the target size, not on a small sample.
Your vector search has 0.98 recall but users still get bad results. Where do you look?
That 0.98 is ANN recall against exact search. Measure retrieval recall@K on labelled queries with exact search: if it is low, the problem is the embedding model, chunking or query (prompt prefix, domain mismatch), not the index. Then check whether hybrid search or a reranker fixes the misses (Pipeline lab).
When is exact search enough?
When the scan fits the latency budget: on one core here, about 0.5 ms for 5,000 vectors of 1,024 dims and about 112 ms for a million. Exact search is also the right choice after a restrictive filter, and as the ground truth for every ANN benchmark.

The two recalls, the before/after lists and the Matryoshka and quantization grid are new runs on those vectors (FAISS 1.15.1 on CPU, one thread for builds, k-means seed fixed; deterministic, no lock). The model comparison comes from the setup's records of record (quality: pytrec_eval; speed: three runs on MPS, load average 1.5 to 11.8 on a shared machine).
  • Re-embedding: only the raw gte-modernbert vectors for the cosine, dot and L2 section (SciFact corpus and 300 claims, MPS, bench lock held).
  • Reused from the Vector indexes child: the Quora frontier (its results.json) and two cross-checks (SQ8 and binary agreement at 1,024 dims).
  • Not run here: a fine-tune of an embedding model (it belongs to the Embedding models child page); DiskANN, ScaNN and filtered search (on the child page); hosted embedding models (no API keys by design).
  • Projection: the 2-D map uses a 705-point sample (seed 0), so trustworthiness and neighbour counts are for that sample.

Agentic lab

Who drives retrieval: a fixed pipeline that searches once, or the model itself, deciding what to search for next. Five ways of answering the same 200 two-hop questions, measured with a small local model: what each gets right, how many searches and tokens it spends, and how long it takes. Then a router that picks between them, long context instead of retrieval, where in a long prompt the evidence gets ignored, a small GraphRAG, and memory.

The running example on this tab
HotpotQA (distractor dev set): 200 questions (160 bridge: find one thing, then a fact about it; 40 comparison: two things compared), each needing two "gold" Wikipedia paragraphs, over a corpus of 9,760 paragraphs. The generator is Qwen3-1.7B (and Qwen3-4B for comparison), 4-bit GGUF in llama.cpp on an Apple M1 Pro, greedy decoding, thinking switched off. The search tool is bge-small-en-v1.5 (exact search, run on the CPU so it does not compete with the generator for the GPU). Every number marked measured was produced here in October 2026; published numbers come from the paper named beside them; constructed marks an input written for this page. Terms (embedding, recall@k, BM25) are defined in the Reading tab; the one-shot pipeline's stages are measured in the Pipeline lab.

Why one search is not enough

A multi-hop question needs facts from more than one passage, and usually the second passage can only be found once the first has been read. "Alexander Kerensky was defeated by the Bolsheviks in a civil war that ended when?" needs one paragraph to learn that the war is the Russian Civil War and a second to learn when it ended. A pipeline searches once, with the question as typed; whatever that one search misses, the generator never sees.

Predict: with bge-small, for how many of the 200 questions are BOTH gold paragraphs in the top 3 of a single search with the question?
122 of 200 (61%). At least one gold paragraph is in the top 3 for nearly every question; the second one is what goes missing. Both are in the top 10 for 164.

The first hop is almost free: some gold paragraph is in the top 10 for 199 of the 200 questions. The second is not: both are in the top 3 for 122 questions with bge-small and 80 with BM25, and in the top 10 for 164 and 147. A pipeline can buy recall by putting more paragraphs in the prompt (top 10 instead of top 3), at a cost in tokens and in distraction; an agent can instead search again for the missing piece, using what it just read. Most second-hop paragraphs here still share a few words with the question (median 3 content words against 4 for the first; only 10 of 200 share none), because HotpotQA questions often name both things: it is the ranking, not total absence, that hides them.

This corpus makes retrieval easy, on purpose
The 9,760 paragraphs are the gold and distractor paragraphs of 1,000 HotpotQA questions, not the 5.2 million paragraphs of the full Wikipedia dump that HotpotQA's "fullwiki" setting and the BEIR benchmark use. A single search finds far more here than it would at full scale (BM25 recall@10 of the gold paragraphs 0.868 here, against recall@100 of 0.740 on BEIR's full HotpotQA corpus). Read the absolute numbers as an easy case; the gaps between strategies are what this tab measures. Qwen3-Embedding lists HotpotQA among its training data, so its HotpotQA results are in-domain, not zero-shot (MTEB model metadata, checked by the Tool map); that is why the search tool here is bge-small, which does not.

Five ways to answer, measured

The same 200 questions, the same corpus, the same search tool, the same generator. Only who decides what to read changes.

1. No retrieval

The question alone. Measures what the model memorised in training ("closed book").

question→generate

2. Single-shot pipeline

Search once with the question, put the top k paragraphs in the prompt, answer. The Pipeline lab's shape. One generator call.

search(question)→top 5→generate

3. Agent loop (ReAct)

The model is given a search tool and decides, step by step, what to search for and when to stop: Thought, Action, Observation, repeated (the ReAct paper's format). At most 4 searches of 3 paragraphs each.

think→search(q1)→read→think→search(q2)→...→finish

4. Decompose, then retrieve

One call splits the question into two sub-questions; each is searched and answered in turn, the first answer filled into the second ("#1"); a last call answers the original question from everything read. A fixed program, not a free loop (the Self-Ask and IRCoT family).

split→search(sub 1)→answer 1→search(sub 2 + #1)→answer

5. Long context

No search: put the gold paragraphs and many distractors straight into the window, as if the whole corpus fitted. Two sizes: the question's own 10 paragraphs (HotpotQA's "distractor" setting, about 1.4k tokens) and about 8k tokens (the own 10 plus the corpus paragraphs nearest the question). The gold paragraphs are always in the window, so this is the best case for long context.

gold + distractors→generate

Each dot is one strategy over the 200 questions, measured. Hollow dots: the same strategy with the other generator. Tokens are what an API would bill (every call's whole prompt plus its output); seconds are wall-clock on this laptop, generator and search together.

Reading the result (Qwen3-4B, the clean comparison). The agent loop is the most accurate retrieval strategy: F1 0.574 against 0.490 for the single-shot pipeline with the top 5, a paired gain of +0.084 (95% interval +0.022 to +0.144; 51 questions better, 24 worse). It pays for it with 2,456 tokens per question against 754 (3.3 times) and 6.15 s against 1.98 s. Decomposition, a fixed two-search program, lands at the pipeline's accuracy (0.488) for 1,993 tokens: on these questions the free loop beat the fixed plan. Without retrieval the 4B model scores 0.193, so most of what it answers comes from what it reads. The agent saw fewer gold paragraphs than the top 5 did (81% against 84%) and still answered better: it reads 3 paragraphs at a time, chosen for the piece it is missing, instead of 5 chosen for the whole question.

Qwen3-1.7B: the loop does not pay. With the smaller model the pipeline (F1 0.402) and the agent loop (0.411) are level: the paired difference is +0.009 with an interval from -0.060 to +0.081, and the loop wins on 48 questions and loses on 53, at 3.3 times the tokens and 3.9 times the seconds. Decomposition is worse than the pipeline (0.335), and the cheapest strong option is to read more: the top 10 scores 0.425 and the question's own 10 paragraphs 0.456. A small model that cannot plan its searches well gains nothing from being allowed to.

A prompt finding along the way
The first 1.7B test runs used an answer prompt that listed "a name, a date, a number, or yes or no" as answer forms. The 1.7B model then answered "yes" or "no" to questions that are not yes/no on 63 of its 200 single-shot answers (F1 0.249); the 4B model, with the same prompt, never did. Held-out tuning had already picked a prompt without that list ("Give only the answer, in as few words as possible"), but a scripting error kept it out of the first test runs. Every one-call 1.7B row on this tab was rerun with the held-out choice; the first runs are kept in the repository as out/strategies_s2prompt.json. The lesson matches the Pipeline lab's: a small generator can collapse onto one answer form, and only held-out checks catch it.

Replay a trajectory: the same question, pipeline against agent

A trajectory is everything an agent did on one question: each thought, each search query, each set of results, the answer. These are the recorded runs, replayed step by step; nothing is re-generated in the page. Switch between the pipeline, the agent loop and decomposition on the same question to see where the evidence comes from, and watch the token counter: every agent step re-sends the whole conversation so far.

Prompt tokens per generator call (light: billed; dark: actually computed, the rest came from the prompt cache)

The questions in the replay are chosen by a fixed rule over the 4B runs, not for a story: the first test question where the agent is right and the pipeline wrong, the first where the reverse happens, a comparison both get right, one where the agent spends all four searches and still fails, one only decomposition gets, and a second agent win. The failures are as instructive as the wins: a loop can search for the wrong entity, repeat a search, or stop early with a plausible guess.

Tokens per step: why agent loops get expensive

A chat model has no memory between calls: each step of the loop sends the system prompt, the question and every earlier thought and observation again. If each step adds about the same number of tokens a, call t carries about t·a tokens and a loop of T calls bills about a·T(T+1)/2: quadratic in the number of steps. A prompt cache (llama.cpp's here; prompt caching at the API providers) stores the attention keys and values of a prefix it has already processed, so only the new tokens are computed; providers bill cached tokens at a discount, not for free. The serving side of this is on Topic: inference-and-serving.

Measured on the 4B runs: the prompt carried into the loop's calls grows from 172 tokens at the first call to 613, 1,077, 1,565 and 2,047 at the fifth, while the prompt cache keeps the tokens actually computed at each call near 450 to 530 (the new observation plus the model's last step). A question that ends in two calls bills 820 input tokens; one that uses all five bills 5,370, 6.5 times as much. And the long trajectories are the failures: the 29 questions that used all four searches score F1 0.18, against 0.673 for the 112 that stopped after two. Repeating a query (36 questions) or losing the format (3 questions; 17 for the 1.7B) is how a small model wastes its budget. A step cap does not just bound cost; past two or three searches, more steps here mostly meant the model was lost.

Long context instead of retrieval

If the model can read 32,768 tokens (Qwen3-1.7B and 4B natively, per their model cards; the 4B up to 131,072 with YaRN; frontier models a million or more), why retrieve at all? Two reasons, both measurable. Cost: every question pays to read the whole window, and prefill time grows faster than linearly with its length (on this laptop the 1.7B model takes about 0.26 s to start answering a 270-token prompt and about 9.3 s for a 7,600-token one, measured by the RAG in production child). Size: this small corpus is 1.34 million Qwen3 tokens; a window of 8,000 holds 0.6% of it. So "long context" below means the best case: the gold paragraphs are always placed in the window, with distractors around them.

Measured with Qwen3-4B: giving the model the question's own 10 paragraphs (2 gold, 8 distractors; about 1,470 prompt tokens) scores F1 0.576, level with the agent loop (0.574) at 60% of its tokens and 3.95 s against 6.15 s. That is the best case: the gold paragraphs are guaranteed to be there, which no real long-context deployment over a corpus can promise. Widen the window to about 8,000 tokens (the same gold paragraphs plus the corpus paragraphs nearest the question) and F1 falls to 0.475, below the five-paragraph pipeline, at 7,963 tokens and 28.8 s per question: more on-topic distractors made the same evidence harder to use. The 1.7B model shows the same pattern: its own 10 paragraphs give its best score of any strategy (F1 0.456, against 0.402 for the top 5 and 0.411 for the agent), and the 8k window drops it to 0.320 at 14.6 s per question.

Lost in the middle, on this model

Liu et al. (2023, "Lost in the Middle", arXiv 2307.03172) found that language models use information at the start and the end of a long prompt better than information in the middle. The test here: the same 20 paragraphs per question (the two gold paragraphs kept together as one block, plus the 18 corpus paragraphs bge-small ranks highest among the rest, so the distractors are on topic), with only the position of the gold block changing.

Predict: for the 4B model, where is accuracy lowest?
In the middle, for the 4B model (100 questions): F1 0.682 with the gold paragraphs first, 0.540 at positions 5 to 6, 0.554 at 10 to 11, 0.599 at 15 to 16 and 0.592 last. The start is clearly best; the dip and the partial recovery at the end are the "lost in the middle" shape, though the middle slots overlap in their intervals.

The 4B model reproduces the shape of Liu et al.'s curve at a smaller scale: a strong advantage for evidence at the very start (0.682) and a drop of 0.13 to 0.14 for evidence in the early middle, with only part of it recovered at the end (0.592). Liu et al. found GPT-3.5-Turbo's end position recovering more (63.2 against 75.8 at the start). The 1.7B model (200 questions) shows the U more clearly: F1 0.496 first, 0.405 and 0.381 in the middle, 0.381 at 15 to 16, and 0.468 last, a drop of 0.115 from the start to the middle; paired over the same questions, first against the middle slot is +0.116 (95% interval +0.063 to +0.168) and last against the middle +0.087 (+0.045 to +0.130). The practical rule: when stuffing a window, put the best evidence first (or last), and measure on your own model before trusting a long prompt to be read evenly.

A router: send each question to the cheapest strategy that can answer it

Most real questions are one-hop ("when was X founded?"), and an agent loop spends several calls on what one search answers. A router looks at the question first and picks the strategy: the one-shot pipeline for one-hop questions, the loop for multi-hop ones. Adaptive-RAG (Jeong et al. 2024, arXiv 2403.14403) trains a small classifier to predict a question's complexity and routes between no retrieval, one step and many steps.

HotpotQA has no one-hop questions, so constructed ones were made: Qwen3-4B read one corpus paragraph (never a gold paragraph of the 200) and wrote one question answerable from it alone, with a short answer copied from the paragraph; questions whose answer was not in the paragraph, was longer than six words or appeared in the question were dropped. Of 240 paragraphs drawn, 198 questions survived the filters (Qwen3-4B, 62,375 tokens, 259 s), split 99 for training and 99 for the test. The mixed test set is 100 of the two-hop questions plus the one-hop test half. Two routers, both trained or prompted without touching the test set: a logistic regression on the question's bge-small vector (the search tool computes it anyway, so routing is free), trained on 400 held-out HotpotQA questions and the one-hop training half; and Qwen3-1.7B asked, with four examples, whether the question needs ONE fact or TWO.

Tokens per question for each policy

Result, with Qwen3-1.7B answering, and it is not the textbook one. Because the 1.7B loop is no better than the pipeline on two-hop questions (F1 0.389 against 0.426 on this half) and worse on one-hop questions (0.515 against 0.599), always using the pipeline is the best simple policy here: F1 0.512 for 766 tokens and 0.92 s per question, against 0.451 for 2,652 tokens and 3.39 s when always using the agent. A router can only help if the loop helps somewhere. The logistic-regression router identifies the question type correctly 74.9% of the time and sends 122 of 199 questions to the loop, which here costs accuracy (F1 0.500) and tokens (1,942). The small model as a router called almost everything one-hop (6 of 199 sent to the loop, 47.7% right), so it behaves like "always pipeline" and lands at 0.520 for 971 tokens. Even a perfect router (0.493 for 1,841 tokens) is below always-pipeline, for the same reason. With the 4B model, whose loop is clearly better on two-hop questions (above), the same router would pay; that run was not made here. Caveat: the one-hop questions are constructed and easier to tell apart than real traffic. Adaptive-RAG's own T5-Large router was right only 54.5% of the time on real mixed benchmarks (table below).

GraphRAG, at small scale

GraphRAG (Edge et al. 2024, Microsoft, arXiv 2404.16130) spends language-model calls at indexing time: it extracts the entities and relations in every chunk into a knowledge graph (nodes are entities, edges are relations), groups the graph into communities (clusters of densely connected entities, found with the hierarchical Leiden algorithm; 600-token chunks and gpt-4-turbo in the paper), and writes a summary of each. At query time, global search answers questions about the whole corpus ("what are the main themes?") by asking every community summary (map) and combining the partial answers (reduce); local search starts from the entities in the question and follows the graph. Plain top-k retrieval cannot answer a corpus-wide question, because no single passage holds the answer. Cheaper variants: LightRAG (Guo et al. 2024, arXiv 2410.05779) keeps the graph but retrieves through entity and relation keywords without community reports; LazyGraphRAG (Microsoft, 2024) defers the language-model work to query time; GraphRAG's own FastGraphRAG extracts noun phrases with ordinary NLP instead of a language model.

Built here measured, small-scale: the own paragraphs of the first 40 test questions, indexed LightRAG-style (Qwen3-1.7B lists entities and relations, one call per paragraph; the paragraph's title is always an entity; entities merged by normalised name), Louvain communities (networkx; Leiden is the same idea with a guarantee of connected communities), and a summary per community of 8 or more entities.

measured Indexing 394 paragraphs that hold 53,062 tokens of text cost 161,797 generator tokens (81,368 in, 80,429 out: about 3 tokens of work per token indexed) and 15.9 minutes of generation on this laptop, plus 36,720 tokens and 99 s to summarise 92 of the 131 communities. The graph has 3,160 entities, only 284 of which appear in more than one paragraph: a small model's names rarely match across paragraphs, which is why real systems add entity resolution. At this rate the whole 9,760-paragraph corpus would take about 6.5 hours of extraction here; the published GraphRAG indexed about 1 million tokens of podcasts in 281 minutes with a hosted model.

Local use: one graph hop to the second paragraph

Seeds are the dense top 2 paragraphs for the question; the graph adds every paragraph that mentions an entity of the seeds or of the question; the additions are ranked by their dense score. Compared with dense alone, on the same 40 questions and the same subset.

Question where the two disagreedense top 3with graph hopgold

With one graph hop, both gold paragraphs are in the top 3 for 29 of the 40 questions against 26 for dense search alone; at the top 2 and the top 5 the two tie (19 and 34). The gain is the bridge case: the second paragraph is reached because it mentions an entity of the first (in the examples, "Viglen" through "Bordan Tkachuk"). Three questions of forty is a small, small-scale result; the child page measures it properly.

Global use: a question about the whole subset

No gold answers exist for these questions, so the two answers are shown side by side, not scored. Largest communities and their summaries:

entitiesmost connectedsummary written by the generator

Answering a corpus-wide question from community summaries costs about 20,000 tokens and 93 calls here, against about 1,500 to 1,900 tokens and one call for top-10 retrieval. The map-reduce answer surveys the largest clusters (and is dominated by them: the biggest communities are about Bharatpur and two sports rivalries), while the retrieval answer describes whichever ten paragraphs were nearest the question's wording. Neither is scored, and the small model makes visible mistakes in both (one global answer puts the Cleveland Browns in the NBA). This is the GraphRAG trade in miniature: a large indexing bill and a larger per-question bill for global questions, in exchange for answers that cover the corpus instead of ten passages.

Go deeper: GraphRAG and structured retrieval (the child page on graphs, communities, LightRAG and when a graph pays for itself) and Agentic retrieval (loops, planners and their failure modes in depth).

Memory: retrieval over the agent's own history

An agent that runs for hours, or across sessions, cannot keep its whole history in the window: the token growth measured above would make every step slower and dearer, and the earliest turns eventually fall out. Agent memory applies retrieval to the agent's own past: turns, tool results and facts it has learned are written to a store, and each step retrieves the few that matter instead of re-reading everything. Everything on this page carries over (chunk the history into turns or facts, embed them, search with the current goal as the query, rerank, and measure whether the needed memory was retrieved), with two differences: the store changes on every step, so writing and forgetting policies matter as much as search, and time matters (a newer fact can overrule an older one). Fact memory, temporal knowledge graphs and OS-style paging are on Agent memory layers; the papers Proactive Memory Agent and Just-in-Time Memory have their own pages; deciding what goes into the window at all is Context engineering.

What transfers to frontier models, and what the papers found

What transfers: the shape. A loop costs several generator calls and a growing prompt per question; a router saves most of that on one-hop traffic; long context pays for every token it reads; a fixed decomposition is cheaper and more predictable than a free loop; an entity graph costs one generator call per chunk before the first question is asked. What does not: the absolute accuracy of a 1.7B or 4B model, and especially how well it follows a tool-use format. Small models fail more at the "agent" part (choosing a good query, knowing when to stop) than at reading; larger models were trained for exactly this and gain more from a loop. Here the 1.7B model gained nothing from the loop (F1 0.411 against 0.402 for the pipeline), while the 4B gained 0.084 and lost the tool format less often (3 questions against 17): the bigger model used the loop better, and only for it would a router pay.
