Common mistakes, and interview questions

Comparing an agent with a pipeline at different reading budgets
An agent that searches four times reads up to 12 paragraphs; a pipeline given the top 3 reads 3. Part of any gain is just more text. Compare at matched paragraphs or tokens too (top 10 here), and report the cost next to the accuracy.
Reporting accuracy without searches, tokens and seconds
A loop that is a few points better at several times the tokens and latency may be the wrong choice for most traffic. Every row on this tab carries its cost; a router is how you get the loop's accuracy where it matters and the pipeline's cost elsewhere.
Counting cached prompt tokens as free
A prompt cache cuts compute and latency for the repeated prefix, but an API still bills cached input tokens (at a discount), and a self-hosted cache costs memory. The quadratic growth of billed tokens with steps remains.
Tuning prompts or the step budget on the test questions
Small generators are very sensitive to the prompt; choosing it on the test set inflates the result. Here every prompt was chosen on held-out questions.
Evaluating with an embedder trained on the benchmark
Qwen3-Embedding lists HotpotQA in its training data; its HotpotQA numbers are in-domain. Check a model's declared training data (MTEB metadata, model cards) before using a benchmark to choose it.
Assuming a long window is read evenly
Position matters: measure accuracy with the evidence at different places before stuffing a window, and put the most relevant passages first or last.
Trusting exact match alone
"October 1922" against "1922", or "Yes" against "yes, both are American": exact match counts these as wrong. ReAct's authors found 29% of their failures were label ambiguity. Report F1 too, and read a sample of failures.

Interview questions, short answers

When do you use an agentic retrieval loop instead of a single retrieve-then-generate pipeline?
When the question needs information you can only know to look for after reading something (multi-hop, comparisons, research tasks), when the first search often fails and needs reformulation, or when the tools vary (search, SQL, an API). Not for one-hop lookups: the loop multiplies calls, tokens and latency. Measure both on a golden set, with cost.
Our agent costs ten times the pipeline. How do you bring it down?
Route: send one-hop questions to the pipeline. Cap steps and stop early when the answer is found. Use prompt caching for the shared prefix. Summarise or drop old observations instead of re-sending them. Retrieve better per step (hybrid search, a reranker) so fewer steps are needed. Use a smaller model for planning queries and a larger one only to answer.
Context windows are a million tokens now. Do we still need RAG?
Usually yes: the corpus is larger than any window, every token in the window is paid for on every question, latency grows with the prompt, models read the middle of long prompts less well, and retrieval gives citations and access control per document. Long context helps when the relevant material is small and changes per question (one contract, one codebase), and the two combine: retrieve generously, then let a long window read it.
How do you evaluate an agentic retrieval system?
Final answers against gold (EM/F1, or a judge where answers are free text), evidence recall (did the needed passages reach the model), and the trajectory: searches, tokens, latency, wasted or repeated steps, format failures. Compare against a single-shot baseline and an oracle (gold passages given) to split retrieval failures from reasoning failures.
When is GraphRAG worth its indexing cost?
When users ask questions about the whole corpus (themes, trends, "what are all the...") that no single passage answers, or when relationships between entities are the point (who worked with whom, supply chains). It costs a model call per chunk before the first question and a rebuild or merge when documents change. For fact lookup, hybrid search with a reranker is cheaper and usually as good; cheaper variants (LightRAG, LazyGraphRAG) move cost to query time.
System design: a research assistant over 2 million internal documents answering multi-step questions. Sketch it.
Ingestion: parse, chunk on structure, embed, BM25 index, metadata and access lists per chunk. Query: a router (a small classifier on the query) sends lookups to hybrid search, reranker, top 5, answer with citations; multi-step questions go to a loop with search as a tool (bounded steps, each search filtered by the user's access), with observations summarised to keep the prompt short and a prompt cache for the fixed prefix. Evaluation: a golden set of both kinds, tracking answer quality, evidence recall, cost and p95 latency per route. Ops: re-index on change, cache frequent queries, log trajectories for failure review.

How this was measured, and the limits

  • Machine: Apple M1 Pro (8 performance and 2 efficiency cores, 16 GB unified memory), llama.cpp build 11146 with Metal for the generator, PyTorch on the CPU for the search tool's query encoder, October 2026. Every generator run held the shared bench lock; the machine was otherwise shared, so seconds carry the load of the day (recorded in the run logs). The ratios between strategies transfer; the seconds do not.
  • Generators: Qwen3-1.7B and Qwen3-4B, 4-bit GGUF (Q4_K_M), temperature 0, seed 0, thinking switched off (enable_thinking: false, documented on both model cards), one request at a time, prompt cache on. Outputs are cached by exact prompt, so every number here is reproducible without rerunning the models.
  • Prompts: each strategy's answer prompt was chosen among two candidates on 60 held-out HotpotQA dev questions (the other 800 questions whose paragraphs are in the corpus), never on the 200 test questions. The Pipeline lab learned why: its first prompt made the 1.7B model answer one label almost always. One asymmetry remains: the 4B single-shot, long-context and position runs used the other candidate answer prompt (the one that listed "yes or no" among the answer forms), because they ran before the prompt-choice bug was found; the 4B made no yes/no mistakes with it, so they were not rerun.
  • Metrics: HotpotQA's official answer normalisation (lowercase, strip punctuation and the articles a, an, the, collapse spaces), exact match and token F1 with its yes/no rule; "gold seen" is the share of the two gold paragraphs that reached any prompt. 95% intervals are bootstrap intervals over questions (2,000 resamples, seed 0); paired differences are per question.
  • Search tool: bge-small-en-v1.5, exact search; the agent is never shown a paragraph twice (each search returns the 3 best paragraphs it has not seen). Search time is milliseconds and is included in seconds per question.
  • Scripts: src/agent/ in the repository; make_data.py builds everything this tab draws, check_numbers.py checks the prose against it.
Not run here, and why
  • The full HotpotQA corpus (5.2 million paragraphs): too large to embed on this laptop; the small corpus makes first-stage retrieval easier, said above.
  • Frontier models: the page runs locally with no API keys; the published table above stands in, labelled.
  • Thinking mode: Qwen3's reasoning mode generates hundreds of tokens per call (about 8 s per answer in the Pipeline lab's test), so a loop of five calls over 200 questions would take hours; every run here has it off.
  • Long context beyond 8k tokens: prefill alone would be about 25 s or more per question for the 1.7B model (extrapolated from the measured 9.3 s at 7.6k tokens).
  • Microsoft's graphrag package: its extraction prompts and thousands of calls are sized for large hosted models; a LightRAG-style extraction with one call per paragraph gives the indexing-cost shape at a scale this laptop can run.
  • Judged answer quality: HotpotQA has gold answers, so EM and F1 are exact; judged metrics belong to RAG and retrieval evaluation; trajectory metrics in depth to Agent and trajectory evaluation.

Tool map

A retrieval system is a stack of separate choices: something that splits documents and wires the steps together (a framework), a model that turns text into vectors (an embedding model), a structure that finds the nearest vectors fast (an ANN index, approximate nearest neighbour), usually wrapped in a vector store that also keeps the text and metadata, a keyword engine (BM25), a second model that re-scores the shortlist (a reranker), and tools that evaluate the result. This tab is a dated atlas of the tools at each layer as of 13 October 2026: who owns each one, its licence, its latest release, whether it is alive, what algorithm it actually runs (read in source or docs, not from marketing pages), and when to choose it.

Where every claim on this tab comes from
measured small real runs on an Apple M1 Pro (CPU) in a separate environment, with the running example's SciFact vectors (bge-small-en-v1.5, made by the setup agent); no timing, so nothing here depends on machine load. source read in the installed package at the version shown, with the file named. docs from the project's own documentation, model card, PyPI or GitHub release page, read on 2026-10-13 and linked. vendor a number the vendor publishes about its own product, not reproduced here. A status the project has not stated (a long silence) is labelled quiet and called an inference.

The database-engine side of the same structures (how pgvector stores HNSW pages, what a filter does to a graph, measured pgvector curves, when to stay in Postgres) belongs to Search and vector databases; this tab does not repeat it and agrees with it. How each index works is taught in the Vector search lab; judged RAG metrics belong to RAG and retrieval evaluation.

The stack, one layer per choice

Read from the top: a question arrives, a framework (or your own code) splits and wires; the embedding model and BM25 turn the question into something searchable; the index finds candidates; a reranker or late-interaction model orders them; an evaluation tool tells you whether any of it worked. Click a layer to filter the atlas below to it.

The one idea to keep
Most of the difference between two vector stores is not the algorithm (nearly all of them run HNSW, the graph index, or a cluster-based IVF index) but the defaults they ship, how they filter, whether hybrid search is built in, and who operates them. The measured section below shows how far the defaults alone move the result on the same vectors.

Atlas

Every card is one tool. Filter by layer, licence, how it is deployed and status; click a card for the details and the sources. Search

Same query, the defaults you get

Here is the claim from the top of the tab, measured. Take the running example's real vectors: the 5,183 SciFact abstracts and the 300 test questions, each turned into a 384-number vector by bge-small-en-v1.5. Give exactly the same vectors to ten libraries and two servers (pgvector and Qdrant in Docker), change nothing, and ask each for the 10 nearest abstracts. Exact search (compare the question with every abstract) defines the right answer; each tool's ANN recall@10 is the share of those 10 it returned. This is the index's recall, not the retrieval's: it asks whether the tool found the true nearest vectors, whatever their relevance. Relevance is the second number, nDCG@10 against SciFact's human labels (a ranking score from 0 to 1 that rewards relevant abstracts near the top; the Pipeline lab teaches it).

The two servers ran in Docker (pgvector/pgvector:pg17, qdrant/qdrant:v1.19.2) on 2026-10-14; recall only, no timing. Scripts src/map/defaults_real.py and defaults_compact.py; vectors from the setup agent (sha256 of corpus.npy recorded in src/map/inputs/defaults_real.json). Chroma and pgvector build their graphs with several threads and LanceDB seeds k-means randomly, so those three move slightly between runs (two runs each: Chroma 0.998 and 0.996, pgvector 0.988 and 0.985, LanceDB IVF_PQ 0.598 and 0.591); the rest repeated exactly. A small corpus: at millions of vectors every index loses more, and the knobs matter more.

Tool and settingIndex actually builtANN recall@10nDCG@10recall@10 (labels)

What it shows. Besides the reference (FAISS Flat), three tools are exact at their defaults: Qdrant's Python client in local mode and Milvus Lite never build an index (they scan), and LanceDB scans until you call create_index(); on a collection this small the Qdrant server scans too (box below). pgvector's HNSW with its default ef_search 40 sits with the other graph indexes. The graph indexes (Chroma, USearch, FAISS HNSW, hnswlib) are close but not exact, and the gap is the search-breadth knob: hnswlib ships ef = 10 and FAISS efSearch = 16, Chroma ef_search = 100. The cluster indexes lose most: FAISS IVF (72 clusters here, the common square-root-of-N choice; FAISS has no default for it) searches only the nearest cluster by default (nprobe 1), and LanceDB's default IVF_PQ compresses each vector, so the ranking inside the shortlist is approximate too. One knob each recovers nearly everything, which is why "we tried X and recall was bad" usually means "we did not set the knob".

Common mistake: benchmarking a mode that never uses the index
Even the Qdrant server scanned here: with defaults it does not build HNSW for a collection under indexing_threshold (10,000 KB), and with the graph built its planner still scans any segment under full_scan_threshold (10,000 KB), so all 5,183 vectors were searched exactly. Only with both lowered did the graph answer (0.996 at the default search breadth, 0.925 at hnsw_ef 16). Small test collections hide the index you will run in production. Qdrant's QdrantClient(":memory:") and Milvus Lite are for development. Both scan every vector, so their recall is perfect and their speed says nothing about the server's index. Milvus Lite even reports HNSW from describe_index after you ask for it, while returning flat-scan results (measured above in the atlas card). Benchmark the server you will run.

Which store?

Choosing a store is mostly choosing an operating model, not an algorithm. Answer six questions; the chooser ranks the stores in the atlas with the reasons that moved each one, every reason linked to the card that sources it. The rules are rules of thumb written for this page from the atlas facts (they are not a benchmark): read the reasons, then measure your top two on your own data, at your own recall target, the way the section above does. For the database-engine side of "stay in Postgres or not", the Search and vector databases page has the memory arithmetic and the measured pgvector curves.

Releases and status, 2016 to 2026

The field moved in three waves: the index algorithms (HNSW 2016, FAISS 2017, DiskANN 2019), then the retrieval models and benchmarks (ColBERT, RAG and BEIR in 2020 and 2021, MTEB in 2022), then the products (every store added HNSW, hybrid search and quantisation between 2023 and 2026). Play the years, or tap a dot. The second view sorts every tool in the atlas by the date of its latest release, which is how "quiet" projects show up.

Tap a dot for the event and its source.

Paper dates are arXiv first versions (checked against the arXiv API by src/map/gen_data.py); release dates are GitHub release publication dates, PyPI upload dates or the project's changelog; every event links its source. "Latest release" is the newest stable version on PyPI or a GitHub release as read on 2026-10-13 (model cards: last revision; hosted APIs: the docs read date, shown hollow).

Reading MTEB and BEIR

Every embedding model is sold with a leaderboard number. Know what it is before trusting it. BEIR (2021) is 18 retrieval datasets used zero-shot: the model is tested on domains it was not trained for, scored by nDCG@10. MTEB (2022) widened this to 8 task types and 58 datasets, of which retrieval is one type; the headline is an average of each task's main score (nDCG@10 for retrieval). MMTEB (2025) grew it to more than 500 tasks in 250+ languages and added smaller benchmarks, among them the English benchmark the leaderboard shows today, MTEB(eng, v2): .

Predict: on SciFact (the running example), how does Qwen3-Embedding-0.6B (596M parameters, June 2025) compare with bge-small-en-v1.5 (33M parameters, 2023)?

Why the headline misleads

  • It averages task types. Retrieval is 10 of the 41 tasks in MTEB(eng, v2); a model can climb on classification and clustering while being average at the retrieval you need. Read the retrieval column, or better, the tasks closest to your domain.
  • Many models trained on the test domains. MTEB records the training data each model declares; a task the model trained on is not zero-shot. The table below is computed here with mteb's own function: most 2024 to 2025 models declare FEVER and HotpotQA training data, whose hard-negative versions are 2 of the 10 retrieval tasks, so their retrieval average is only 80% zero-shot. (HotpotQA is also the Agentic lab's multi-hop set: with these models it is in-domain, not zero-shot.)
  • Versions are not comparable. OpenAI's 62.3% and 64.6% for text-embedding-3 are on the 2024 MTEB; Google's 68.x for gemini-embedding-001 is on its own table; today's leaderboard is MTEB(eng, v2). Put only numbers from the same benchmark version side by side.
  • Differences are often noise. Google's own table gives gemini-embedding-001 68.16 at 2048 dimensions and 68.17 at 1536: a smaller vector scoring higher is what noise looks like. A 0.5-point gap between two models is not a reason to switch.
  • Results are often submitted by the model's authors. The MTEB results repository holds runs by the MTEB team and runs supplied by model authors (the setup agent found bge-small's HotpotQA score only in an "external" folder). The running example reproduced bge-small's SciFact score exactly (nDCG@10 0.7127, measured here): reproduction is possible, so do it for the models you shortlist.
  • Your corpus is not the benchmark. The predict question above is the point: on SciFact the 33M model beats the 0.6B one, on NFCorpus it is the other way round, and a 149M model beats both on SciFact. Shortlist with the leaderboard, decide with a golden set of your own questions (the Pipeline lab builds one).

Checks and limits

  • Run here (Apple M1 Pro, CPU, a separate Python 3.12 environment): install and import of every open-source Python package in the atlas; tiny index-and-search checks for FAISS, hnswlib, USearch, Chroma, Qdrant's local mode, LanceDB, Milvus Lite, bm25s, rank_bm25 and ranx (src/map/checks_stores.py, synthetic vectors); the defaults experiment on the running example's real vectors (defaults_real.py); framework defaults read from the installed source (checks_frameworks.py); mteb zero-shot metadata.
  • Not run here, and why. No hosted service (Pinecone, turbopuffer, OpenAI, Gemini, Voyage, Cohere): this topic runs locally with no paid APIs or keys, so their rows are from docs. No server-mode Qdrant, Milvus, Weaviate, Elasticsearch, OpenSearch, Vespa or Redis: Docker servers were left to the setup agent's confirmation, and the engine view of pgvector is measured on the Search and vector databases page. No timing at all on this tab: speed claims are the vendors', labelled.
  • How versions and dates were read. PyPI JSON API (upload time of the version's first file), GitHub REST API (release published_at; the Atom feeds were not used for dates because their "updated" field changes when a release note is edited: hnswlib v0.9.0 shows 2026-09-13 there but was published 2026-03-28), Hugging Face model API (licence tag, revision, parameters from safetensors metadata), arXiv API. Raw records are in src/map/inputs/; gen_data.py re-checks every timeline date against them.
  • Statuses. "active", "maintenance" and "superseded" quote the project or follow from a newer generation by the same owner; "quiet" means no release for many months with no statement, and is an inference. Re-check any tool before you depend on it: this atlas is a snapshot.
  • Licences. Read from PyPI metadata, the repository's LICENSE file and model cards. GitHub reports NOASSERTION for pgvector, Weaviate, Elasticsearch and Redis because their licence files are not a single standard text; the atlas states what the files say.

Interview questions

We moved from FAISS Flat to a vector database and answer quality dropped. What do you check first?
The defaults, in order: the search breadth (ef, ef_search, nprobe; hnswlib ships ef = 10, FAISS IVF nprobe = 1); the distance metric and normalisation (Chroma defaults to l2 when you pass your own vectors); compression without rescoring (an IVF_PQ index without a refine step returned 0.59 of the exact top 10 here); filters applied after the search (fewer than k results survive); and whether you benchmarked a local or "lite" mode that does not use the index at all. Measure ANN recall@10 against exact search on a sample, then retrieval recall on a golden set.
pgvector, Qdrant or Pinecone for a 20M-chunk, multi-tenant SaaS?
Ask where the data lives, how selective the tenant filter is, and who operates it. If tenants' documents already live in Postgres and the index fits one server's memory, pgvector keeps one transaction and one backup, with partitions per large tenant. If tenant filters are very selective or you need hybrid dense plus sparse in one query, Qdrant's in-graph filtering and Query API fit. If nobody can operate a database, Pinecone's namespaces per tenant. Then load a sample into the top two and measure recall at the real filter rate.
How do you choose an embedding model?
Shortlist on the retrieval tasks of MTEB closest to your domain, not the average; check the zero-shot share and the licence (several strong models are non-commercial); check context length against your chunk size and dimension against your memory budget (Matryoshka models let you shorten vectors); then measure nDCG@10 and recall@100 on a golden set of your own questions. Remember queries may need an instruction or prefix.
Is the top model on MTEB the best for us?
Not necessarily: the headline averages task types, many models trained on the benchmarks' training splits, and gaps under a point are within noise. On SciFact a 33M model beat a 0.6B one. Use the leaderboard to shortlist and your own data to decide.
When is GraphRAG worth its indexing cost?
When questions are about the whole corpus ("what are the main themes across these reports") and no single chunk answers them. GraphRAG pays LLM calls at indexing time to build and summarise an entity graph; LightRAG and FastGraphRAG cut that bill; LazyGraphRAG (Microsoft's products only) defers it to query time. For fact lookups, plain hybrid retrieval with a reranker is cheaper and as good; the Agentic lab measures a small case.
Hybrid search: rank fusion or score fusion?
Rank fusion (RRF) ignores the scores and only uses positions, so it needs no calibration between BM25 and cosine scores; Qdrant's Query API, LanceDB's default hybrid reranker and Elasticsearch's rrf retriever all implement it. Score fusion (Weaviate's default relative score fusion, OpenSearch's normalization processor) can use how confident each side is, but moves when the score distributions change. Start with RRF; tune the weights only with a golden set.
